Article Title: Meet Jo Nagai: 10-year-old Japanese student who discovered butterflies can remember their time as caterpillars after he noticed that the caterpillars he had raised to recognise him after turning into
Article Text:
Who is Jo Nagai, the 10-year-old Japanese student behind the butterfly discovery?



The observation that started Jo Nagai's butterfly research

What did Jo Nagai's butterfly experiments reveal?

Possible evidence of inherited butterfly memories



How scientists are viewing Jo Nagai's findings

Why Jo Nagai's butterfly research went viral

The scientific significance of Jo Nagai's discovery

A 10-year-old student from Japan has captured worldwide attention after his fascination with butterflies led to a remarkable scientific study that is challenging long-held assumptions about insect memory. Jo Nagai, an elementary school student from Kobe, spent years carefully observing the Asian swallowtail butterflies he raised at home. His curiosity was sparked when he noticed that the butterflies appeared to recognise him even after undergoing metamorphosis from caterpillars. Determined to understand whether memories formed during the caterpillar stage could survive this dramatic transformation, Jo designed a series of experiments that have since been presented before professional scientists, generating discussions about animal cognition, metamorphosis and inherited behaviour. While some of his findings still require independent verification, his work has made him one of the youngest researchers to gain international recognition.Jo Nagai is a 10-year-old student at Ibuki East Elementary School in Kobe, Japan. He is also a scholar of the Son Masayoshi Philanthropic Foundation, which supports exceptionally talented young people across the country. Passionate about insects since early childhood, Jo has reportedly filled hundreds of handwritten pages with observations of insect behaviour.Despite gaining international recognition for his butterfly research, he says his long-term ambition is to become a veterinarian, reflecting his lifelong love for animals and nature.Jo's research did not begin in a laboratory or as part of a school assignment. Instead, it started with a simple observation while raising Asian swallowtail butterflies. He noticed that wild butterflies usually flew away when approached, but the butterflies he had raised from caterpillars often returned to his hand even after being released into the wild. This unusual behaviour led him to wonder whether butterflies could retain memories formed during their caterpillar stage despite undergoing complete metamorphosis. Motivated by that question, he spent several years documenting their behaviour and developing carefully planned experiments.To investigate his hypothesis, Jo exposed swallowtail caterpillars to the scent of lavender while simultaneously applying a mild vibration stimulus using a muscle-therapy device. After the caterpillars completed metamorphosis and emerged as butterflies, he tested them using a Y-shaped tube maze. According to his findings, around 70% of the adult butterflies avoided the lavender scent, suggesting they had retained memories formed before metamorphosis. These observations challenge the traditional belief that an insect's nervous system is completely rebuilt during the pupal stage, erasing all previous memories. His findings add to a growing body of scientific research suggesting that some forms of memory may survive metamorphosis.One of the most striking aspects of Jo's research involved studying later generations of butterflies. After breeding the conditioned butterflies, he reported that their offspring and even grandchildren also showed an increased tendency to avoid the lavender scent despite never being exposed to the original conditioning. He suggested that this behaviour could be explained through transgenerational epigenetic inheritance, a process in which environmental experiences may influence later generations without changing DNA sequences. However, scientists emphasise that this conclusion remains preliminary and will require further independent studies before it can be accepted as established scientific evidence.Jo's work has attracted considerable interest because it aligns with an emerging field of research exploring how insect memories survive metamorphosis. His study has been presented at scientific meetings, including the International Congress of Entomology in Kobe, where professional entomologists reviewed his findings. Although the research has generated significant discussion within the scientific community, it has not yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal. Experts regard his work as an impressive contribution from a young researcher while noting that replication by independent scientists will be essential to confirm the results.Jo's story has spread rapidly across social media because it combines childhood curiosity with genuine scientific investigation. Many people have been amazed that a 10-year-old produced a detailed 33-page research paper and presented his findings before experienced scientists. Videos of his presentations and summaries of his work have attracted millions of views online, with many praising his dedication, patience and scientific thinking. At the same time, some users questioned the ethics of using an aversive stimulus on caterpillars, prompting debates about the methods used during the experiments. Others defended the study, noting that the procedures were designed to trigger natural defensive responses rather than intentionally harm the insects.If future research confirms Jo's findings, they could deepen scientists' understanding of insect memory, metamorphosis and the possible role of epigenetics in transmitting learned behaviours across generations. His work also highlights how careful observation and curiosity can lead to meaningful scientific questions regardless of age. Beyond its scientific implications, Jo Nagai's story has become an inspiring example of how young minds can contribute to real-world research, encouraging children around the world to pursue their curiosity, ask thoughtful questions and explore science through observation and experimentation.
Article Summary: Jo Nagai is a 10-year-old student at Ibuki East Elementary School in Kobe, Japan. He spent years observing the Asian swallowtail butterflies he raised at home. His curiosity was sparked when he noticed that the butterflies appeared to recognise him even after undergoing metamorphosis from caterpillars. He designed a series of experiments that have since been presented before professional scientists, generating discussions about animal cognition and inherited behaviour.

Article Title: Watch: Viral video of dolphin carrying its dead newborn through the Indian Ocean reveals a deep and old 'mourning ritual'
Article Text:
Fraggle, a grieving mother dolphin, carried her deceased calf for six days, a poignant testament to her profound maternal love. Captured by drone footage in the Indian Ocean, this heart-wrenching scene revealed the support of her pod, which gathered around her in solidarity during her mourning. This behavior, seen in over twenty cetacean species, underscores their intricate social connections and possible awareness of mortality.

How do dolphins mourn?

Tahlequah, an orca mother who carried her dead newborn around for an astonishing seventeen days, travelling up to 1,000 miles

Social media reactions

In a video going viral on the internet and capturing hearts online, a grieving mother dolphin named Fraggle carried her dead calf through the Indian Ocean for six days. Drone footage captured by Geographe Marine Research, an Australian conservation organisation, showed the mother dolphin with her newborn, which was only two weeks old.What had viewers grieving and emotional was the revelation that Fraggle had previously experienced the loss of four other calves. Other dolphins were observed joining the mother during her period of mourning. Her entire pod of 14 dolphins came to support Fraggle, named after the muppet in Fraggle Rock, riding by her side to support her through her heartbreak.Researchers noted the calf showed a high breathing rate before dying and winter births in the region are known to pose major survival hurdles, often linked to respiratory complications from cold air. Researchers have documented similar grief-like behaviour in dolphins and whales, where they carry their deceased offspring.As an inevitable part of nature, death happens to all beings. Despite the certainty of it, coping with death is never easy and different for everyone. Animals including elephants, apes, and cetaceans all react differently when they lose a group member or a family member.Several species of cetaceans have been observed behaving in ways that suggest they mourn their dead group members.Some dolphin mothers carry around their calves on their backs for hours or even days. The most heartbreaking tale is that of Tahlequah, an orca mother who carried her dead newborn around for an astonishing seventeen days, travelling up to 1,000 miles, until she finally let it go six feet under. In a 2018 study published in Zoology, scientists found that at least 20 species of cetaceans display some form of “post-mortem attentive behaviour” (in human societies, we might interpret these as grief). Of the 20 species, most were dolphins rather than whales. Following the “social brain hypothesis,” animals with complex social structures, i.e., dolphins, generally have relatively bigger brains. A big brain relates to more complex feelings and perhaps an understanding of the concept of death, to some extent.Carrying a dead body around for a prolonged time is energetically costly, it breaks streamlined body shape, stops the hunt for prey and is generally taxing. Then why do dolphin mothers keep carrying around and pushing their loved ones? Could they think the calf is simply unconscious, and it still has a chance if they help it breathe at the surface? Altruistic acts like these aren’t uncommon in social species. Post-mortem attentive behaviour could be beyond evolutionary explanation and simply be a reflection of the strong bond between a mother and her calf.There are many similarities in how some cetaceans react to dead conspecifics and how humans deal with the passing away of a loved one. On the other hand, “grieving” is not a ubiquitous event in cetacean societies: many times, when an individual dies, the rest of the pod leaves the body behind and moves on with their lives. So, cetaceans don't behave exactly like grieving humans but may have similar inspirations upon such events.As the video gained traction online, numerous viewers shared emotional comments over the visual."Grief is the price we pay for loving deeply" wrote a user on Reddit."That was the whole family grieving with her" added another."Dolphins and orcas' emotional centre of the brain is a larger percentage of the brain than they are in humans. Possibly implying we literally can't fathom the depths of their sadness when losing a child. That's already the worst pain imaginable for a parent, but still might not compare to what they're feeling," shared a user."There’s no greater pain than a mother mourning their child. I would never wish it on my worst enemy" another wrote.
Article Summary: A grieving mother dolphin named Fraggle carried her dead calf through the Indian Ocean for six days. Drone footage captured by Geographe Marine Research, an Australian conservation organisation, showed the mother dolphin with her newborn, which was only two weeks old. Other dolphins were observed joining the mother during her period of mourning.

Article Title: A rare yellow-flowered California plant unseen since 1957 has been rediscovered after 68 years
Article Text:
Representative Image of a long-lost California wildflower found again after decades (AI-generated image)

How botanists rediscovered a flower missing for nearly 70 years

Why the plant had gone undetected for so long

What role grazing plays on this land more broadly

Why this rediscovery matters for conservation in the region

A small, yellow-flowered California native plant that had not been documented in nearly seven decades has been rediscovered in the hills of eastern Contra Costa County. The caper-fruited Tropidocarpum, last recorded in 1957, was found on March 3, 2025, by botanist Heath Bartosh of Nomad Ecology and his colleague Spencer Adams, working on behalf of the East Contra Costa County Habitat Conservancy. The discovery was made on protected land within Vasco Hills Regional Preserve, acquired jointly by the East Bay Regional Park District and the conservancy, and comes after a deliberate, sustained search for the plant rather than a chance sighting.According to East Bay Parks' own account of the discovery, Bartosh was specifically searching local ridgetops for caper-fruited tropidocarpum when he and Adams located the population, work carried out on behalf of the East Contra Costa County Habitat Conservancy. The search was prompted by an earlier sighting of a few individual plants on nearby private land in 2023, which gave botanists reason to believe a larger population might still survive somewhere in the surrounding hills.Finding the plant required more than a single visit to the right location. According to conservancy executive director Abigail Fateman, documenting the new population required a thoughtful survey approach and persistence, since annual plants like this one do not necessarily germinate every year, meaning a site could appear empty in one season and still support the species in another.The caper-fruited tropidocarpum was first documented in 1888 by University of California, Berkeley botany professor Edward Lee Greene, who described it at the time as common in the low alkaline valley lands skirting the San Joaquin River. According to Bartosh, the plant's decline traces back largely to competition from non native species that have become increasingly dominant across California grasslands since the late 1880s, gradually crowding out native plants like this one from the habitat they once occupied freely.The species is currently listed as 1B.1 by the California Native Plant Society, a designation indicating it is considered rare, threatened or endangered both within California and elsewhere. Even with this newly confirmed population, there remain only two known populations of the plant across the entire East Bay region, each consisting of fewer than 20 individual plants.While this specific rediscovery is attributed to a targeted botanical survey rather than land management practices, grazing does play a documented role in shaping native plant communities on East Bay Regional Park District land more generally. A peer-reviewed study published in the journal PLOS ONE titled Livestock grazing supports native plants and songbirds in a California annual grassland , funded in part by the East Bay Regional Park District, found that livestock grazing on California annual grasslands was associated with higher native plant cover and shorter, less dense vegetation compared to ungrazed areas, since removing built-up grass litter and reducing the height of invasive annual grasses can give native species more room to establish and compete.This kind of research helps explain why land managers across the East Bay increasingly treat grazing as one tool among several for maintaining grassland habitat, alongside targeted surveys, invasive species removal and permanent land protection, even though this particular plant's rediscovery is credited specifically to focused fieldwork rather than any single land management intervention.The Vasco Hills Regional Preserve sits within a roughly 14,000-acre area of eastern Contra Costa County managed through a partnership between the East Bay Regional Park District and the East Contra Costa County Habitat Conservancy. According to Park District General Manager Sabrina Landreth, the discovery illustrates the value of that partnership, reflecting a shared effort between the two agencies to protect sensitive species while also maintaining public access and recreation opportunities across the land they jointly manage.With the newly confirmed population now identified, conservancy staff have said it will become a high priority for ongoing monitoring and management, given how few populations of the species are known to survive and how easily an annual plant like this one could go undetected again if survey efforts were not maintained consistently in the years ahead.
Article Summary: The caper-fruited Tropidocarpum, last recorded in 1957, was found on March 3, 2025, by botanist Heath Bartosh of Nomad Ecology and his colleague Spencer Adams. The discovery was made on protected land within Vasco Hills Regional Preserve, acquired jointly by the East Bay Regional Park District and the East Contra Costa County Habitat Conservancy.

Article Title: Florida's first flesh-eating bacteria death of 2026 raises concerns during beach season as warm waters fuel infections
Article Text:
Image Credit: CDC/ Janice Haney Carr

What is Florida ’s flesh-eating bacteria that killed its first target

Map illustrating the distribution ofVibrio vulnificus infections along the coastal United States. Image Credit: nature.com

How can people come in contact with this infection

Who is at the highest risk from this disease

Image Credit: CDC/James Gathany

What are the possible symptoms to look out for

Ways of protection during the visit at the beach

Why is weather an important factor in these outbreaks

Florida health authorities have officially confirmed the state's first fatality of 2026 linked to Vibrio vulnificus, a naturally occurring ‘flesh-eating bacteria’. This specific death involved a resident of Palm Beach County aged between 80-84 years. According to the BEACON(public health program based at Boston University) , these cases are distributed across the Gulf and Atlantic coasts, including areas such as Hillsborough, Lee, and Miami-Dade.While the total number of infections are slightly below the figures seen during the previous hurricane-filled years, the doubling of case counts since June highlights a significant seasonal peak. Health officials point out that the bacterium prosper in warm, brackish coastal waters, particularly between May and October. Public awareness is of utmost importance as the state enters the peak of the summer recreation and hurricane season.Vibrio vulnificus is a bacterium that naturally lives in coastal environments, particularly salt water and brackish water (a mixture of fresh and salt water). Information provided by University of South Florida clarifies that the bacterium does not actually ‘eat’ flesh in a literal sense. It produces toxins that cause the surrounding skin and soft tissue to die.These organisms are highly adaptable when water temperatures rise, making Florida’s coastal regions a primary habitat. As per the National Library of Medicine , global climate change has allowed this bacterium to expand towards further north, but the warm, salty waters of the Gulf Coast remain its favorite home.There are two primary ways a person might come into contact with this dangerous bacterium. The first is through the consumption of contaminated food, specifically raw or undercooked shellfish like oysters. Oysters can concentrate the bacteria within their tissues, making them particularly hazardous if eaten raw.The second common reason for infection is when an open wound gets exposed to seawater or brackish water containing the bacteria. It is important to remember that ‘open wounds’ are not just large cuts, even tiny scratches, recent surgical sites, new piercings, or fresh tattoos can provide an entry point for the infection.According to the Florida Department of Health, individuals with weakened immune systems are at a substantially higher risk. This includes people living with chronic liver disease, cancer, diabetes, HIV, or those receiving treatments that suppress the immune system.University of South Florida reports that a recent study found people with these pre-existing conditions were eighty times more likely to develop this infection from this bacterium than healthy individuals. Furthermore, men over the age of forty appear to be more vulnerable, because of a higher prevalence of liver disease within that age group.If the bacteria were swallowed, a person might experience gastrointestinal distress, such as watery diarrhoea, stomach cramps, nausea, vomiting, fever, and chills. However, if the infection begins in a wound, the signs are often more visible and aggressive.The Hillsborough Community Health Newsletter lists redness, intense pain, swelling, and warmth as early indicators. This can rapidly progress to the formation of fluid-filled blisters, known as bullae, which often turn a dark purple colour. Because these infections can spread through the individual within just 1-2 days, every hour counts when seeking help.The Centre for Disease Control(CDC) and the Florida Department of Health in St. Johns County recommend staying out of salt or brackish water entirely if you have any open cuts or wounds. If you must go near the water, ensure any breaks in the skin are completely covered with a waterproof bandage. After swimming or handling raw seafood, always wash your skin thoroughly with soap and clean, running water.For those who enjoy seafood, the advice is clear to ‘avoid raw oysters and shellfish.’ Only cooking these items to the correct temperature will kill the bacteria.The bacteria thrive in warm water, which is why cases typically peak between May and October. However, extreme weather events like hurricanes play a significant role in sudden surges of the disease. Hurricanes Ian in 2022 and Helene in 2024 both led to an unusual increase in cases because storm surges pushed brackish water into inland areas, exposing many people during evacuations and clean-up efforts.The BEACON report notes that while 2026 has been relatively quiet so far regarding major storms, the doubling of cases in the mid-summer months indicates that the seasonal heat alone is enough to drive bacterial growth. Given that bloodstream infections are fatal roughly 50% of the time, the message from all health agencies is ‘do not wait.’ Early intervention is the most effective tool in surviving this rare but dangerous bacterium.
Article Summary: Vibrio vulnificus is a naturally occurring ‘flesh-eating bacteria’ The bacterium does not actually ‘eat’ flesh in a literal sense. It produces toxins that cause the surrounding skin and soft tissue to die. Bacterium prosper in warm, brackish coastal waters, particularly between May and October.

Article Title: Most ancient Arctic carbon entering the ocean gets buried instead of becoming greenhouse gas, study finds
Article Text:
Representative Image of thawing Arctic permafrost releasing ancient carbon into coastal waters (AI-generated image)

How much carbon is actually entering the Arctic Ocean

What the sediment cores from Herschel Island revealed

How researchers tracked exactly where the carbon came from

Why "gourmet" bacteria may be limiting the climate impact

Why this carbon movement could still reshape Arctic ecosystems

As Arctic permafrost thaws and coastlines erode, enormous quantities of ancient carbon that has sat frozen in the ground for thousands of years are being carried into the sea. Scientists have long worried that microorganisms in the ocean would break this carbon down and release it as greenhouse gases, adding a dangerous new feedback loop to climate change. A new study led by researchers at the Alfred Wegener Institute and MARUM, the Centre for Marine Environmental Sciences at the University of Bremen, has found a more reassuring picture, at least for now. Examining sediment cores collected off the coast of Qikiqtaruk, also known as Herschel Island, in Canada, the team found that the vast majority of this land-based carbon simply becomes buried in the seafloor, with only around 10 per cent converted into greenhouse gases.According to the Alfred Wegener Institute, Arctic permafrost ecosystems hold roughly 1,300 gigatonnes of organic carbon on land, much of it made up of ancient plant remains, with a further 400 gigatonnes already stored in ocean sediments and river deltas. Because the Arctic is warming faster than any other region on the planet, this frozen carbon store has become increasingly vulnerable, as thawing ground and eroding coastlines allow carbon to escape into the Arctic Ocean via rivers and coastal breakdown.Study lead author Dr Manuel Ruben of the Alfred Wegener Institute said up to 0.02 gigatonnes of this carbon are already entering the sea each year, and that forecasts suggest this outflow could rise by 70 to 150 per cent by 2100. Until now, Ruben said, how much of that carbon eventually returns to the atmosphere as a greenhouse gas, versus how much stays locked in the ocean, had remained largely unknown, despite being essential information for building accurate climate models.To answer this question, researchers collected sediment cores from several locations along the coast of Herschel Island, each containing layers of material built up over roughly 50 years. According to the study published in Nature Geoscience titled Limited remineralisation of Arctic permafrost-derived organic carbon in nearshore marine sediments , the results showed that only a relatively small share of the carbon swept into the ocean actually becomes part of the ocean's active carbon cycle, meaning most of it is not immediately available for microorganisms to break down and release as gas.Ruben said that although the sea carries away huge quantities of organic carbon from the coast, surprisingly little of it ends up cycling actively through the system. Microorganisms convert roughly 10 per cent of the organic carbon found in the sediments into gases that rise into the surrounding water and can eventually reach the atmosphere, while the remaining carbon stays buried within the seabed itself.To work out precisely where the carbon in the sediment had originated, the team analysed dissolved inorganic carbon trapped in pore water, the tiny spaces between individual sediment particles, since this reveals how much carbon dioxide microorganisms have released after consuming organic material. According to the Alfred Wegener Institute, the isotopic makeup of that pore water then allowed researchers to trace exactly where the consumed material had come from.Professor Gesine Mollenhauer, a geochemist at AWI and co-spokesperson for the Cluster of Excellence The Ocean Floor: Earth's Unexplored Interface, explained that carbon isotopes function as atomic indicators of an organism's food source. The 13C isotope reveals whether microorganisms had consumed carbon originating from land or from the sea, while the 14C isotope allowed the team to determine whether these single-celled organisms preferred old organic carbon from permafrost or fresher organic carbon from more recent algae remains.The isotope analysis revealed a clear pattern in what the seabed's microorganisms actually preferred to eat. According to Mollenhauer, the sediment is home to what she described as gourmet bacteria that clearly prefer fresh carbon, such as that from recent algal remains, over the older carbon released from thawing permafrost deposits. Because these microbes favour fresher marine material over ancient permafrost carbon, the researchers concluded that permafrost carbon may end up contributing less to atmospheric greenhouse gas levels than scientists had previously feared.The research team was careful to note that this reassuring picture remains incomplete. Some of the organic carbon released from permafrost may already be broken down before it ever reaches the seabed, meaning further research is still needed to build a full accounting of the carbon's journey from thawing land to the ocean floor.Beyond its implications for greenhouse gas emissions, the movement of carbon from land into the ocean carries other consequences for coastal Arctic ecosystems. According to the Alfred Wegener Institute, sediment released through coastal erosion can reduce how much sunlight reaches the water, since freshly eroded material makes coastal water cloudier while dissolved organic carbon can darken it further. That reduced light availability can in turn affect single-celled algae that rely on sunlight to produce biomass and oxygen, organisms that sit at the base of a food web supporting fish, crustaceans and seals relied upon by local communities.Researchers plan to investigate these broader ecosystem effects further during the international Arctic Pulse campaign scheduled for 2027, which will involve coordinated observations from the Polarstern research icebreaker, AWI research aircraft and monitoring sites on land, aimed at understanding how rapidly changing Arctic conditions are reshaping the region's ecosystems as a whole. In the meantime, Ruben said the current findings provide a far more precise picture than previously available of exactly how much carbon is being safely stored in the seabed, and how much of the carbon being broken down genuinely originates from ancient permafrost, offering climate modellers a stronger foundation for predicting the true consequences of continued permafrost thaw.
Article Summary: Arctic permafrost is thawing and coastlines are eroding, allowing carbon to escape into the Arctic Ocean via rivers and coastal breakdown. Scientists have long worried that microorganisms in the ocean would break this carbon down and release it as greenhouse gases. A new study led by researchers at the Alfred Wegener Institute and MARUM in Bremen has found a more reassuring picture, at least for now.

Article Title: Washington family receives $350,000 after a river otter dragged their toddler underwater and attacked the child’s mother
Article Text:
A river otter dragged a toddler into the water and bit his mother at Bremerton Marina in 2024. The family has now reached a $350,000 settlement with the Port of Bremerton. (representative image)

What happened at the marina?

Why the lawsuit mattered

Why this attack stands out

What happened afterward

A Washington family has reached a $350,000 settlement after a rare river otter attack at Bremerton Marina left a toddler injured and the child’s mother bitten during the rescue. The case has now been dismissed, with the Port of Bremerton agreeing to settle without admitting fault, as reported by KOIN 6.According to reports from state wildlife officials, the incident happened on September 12, 2024, when a river otter grabbed the toddler and pulled the child off a dock and into the water. The child resurfaced moments later, and when the mother pulled the toddler out, the otter continued attacking and bit her arm.The toddler was treated at a hospital in Silverdale for scratches and bite wounds on the head, face, and legs. The lawsuit also said both the mother and child later underwent rabies shots.The family argued that otters had already been reported as a nuisance at the marina more than a year before the attack and claimed the Port of Bremerton failed to keep the area safe. The port rejected those claims, saying it had not received reports of aggressive otters and disputing that security around the docks was inadequate,as per KOIN 6.Under the settlement, 40% of the $350,000 is set aside for attorneys’ fees and related costs, while the family’s share will go into a trust and be paid through the port’s insurance company, reported USA Today.River otter attacks on humans are rare, which is part of why this case drew so much attention. Washington wildlife officials have said only a small number of human-river otter incidents have been documented in the state over the past decade.The setting also mattered: this was not a remote wildlife encounter but a developed marina, where people and animals came into close contact. Experts note that conflicts become more likely when human spaces overlap with wildlife habitat, as per a BBC Future report.After the attack, state wildlife officers worked with U.S. Department of Agriculture Wildlife Services to trap and remove otters from the marina. One otter was captured and later tested negative for rabies.The Port of Bremerton said the settlement was a compromise of disputed and uncertain claims and expressed sympathy for the family, calling it a very unfortunate accident.
Article Summary: A Washington family has reached a $350,000 settlement after a rare river otter attack at Bremerton Marina left a toddler injured and the child's mother bitten during the rescue. The family argued that otters had already been reported as a nuisance at the marina more than a year before the attack. The case has now been dismissed, with the Port of BreMERton agreeing to settle without admitting fault.

Article Title: The US plans to auction up to 33 million acres of deep ocean around American Samoa for mineral exploration despite major environmental data gaps
Article Text:
The US plans to auction up to 33 million acres of deep ocean around American Samoa for mineral exploration despite major environmental data gaps

Two lease blocks identified for exploration

Why the US is interested in deep-sea minerals

What companies would be allowed to do

Environmental concerns remain

American Samoa groups oppose the proposal

What happens next?

The United States has moved a step closer to deep-sea mining after the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) proposed auctioning two massive seabed lease areas near American Samoa for mineral exploration. The proposal marks a significant milestone in the country's efforts to secure critical mineral supplies for clean energy, electronics and national security.The proposed lease blocks together span approximately 31.5 million acres within a broader 33 million-acre study area, making it one of the largest offshore mineral leasing initiatives undertaken by the U.S. If approved, the lease sale is scheduled for November 19, 2026.However, the proposed auction would not authorize companies to begin commercial mining. Instead, successful bidders would only be allowed to conduct preliminary exploration activities, including geological surveys, seabed sampling and oceanographic measurements. Any future extraction of minerals would require separate federal approvals, detailed mining plans and additional environmental reviews.According to BOEM, the proposed lease areas cover 16.3 million acres and 15.2 million acres, respectively. The agency said the sale is still subject to legal procedures and public consultation, meaning the auction could be modified or cancelled before it takes place.The seabed in the proposed leasing area lies at depths ranging from about 4,600 feet to 20,000 feet. Portions of the zone are located roughly 57 miles from Rose Atoll, although BOEM said the lease blocks do not overlap the Rose Atoll National Wildlife Refuge or the surrounding marine national monument.Deep-sea deposits are believed to contain valuable minerals such as copper, nickel, cobalt and manganese, which are essential for manufacturing electric vehicle batteries, renewable energy technologies, consumer electronics and defence equipment."Critical minerals have become a strategic asset in global competition," said Matt Giacona, acting director of the Marine Minerals Administration.The proposed leasing programme aligns with the Trump administration's strategy to reduce U.S. dependence on overseas mineral supply chains, particularly those linked to China.An executive order signed in April 2025 directed federal agencies to accelerate seabed mineral development. In January 2026, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) streamlined its permitting process by allowing companies to apply simultaneously for exploration licences and commercial recovery permits through a consolidated application.If the leases are awarded, companies will initially be permitted to conduct geophysical mapping of the seabed, limited geological and biological sampling, oceanographic measurements, and studies of marine habitats, ocean currents and biodiversity.Industrial-scale mineral extraction would not be permitted under the initial leases.Officials say the surveys are intended to gather scientific data and assess mineral resources before any mining proposals are considered.The proposal has sparked criticism from scientists, environmental organisations and community groups, who argue that even preliminary leasing could pave the way for future commercial mining in one of Earth's least understood ecosystems.Researchers warn that large-scale deep-sea mining could generate underwater noise, artificial light and sediment plumes capable of disturbing fragile marine habitats that have evolved in darkness for millions of years.Although BOEM's environmental assessment concluded that the proposed exploration activities are unlikely to cause significant adverse impacts, it also acknowledged that biodiversity and ecological conditions in the region remain poorly understood.Critics argue that commercial leasing should not move forward until more scientific data is available.Community organisations in American Samoa have also voiced opposition, saying the surrounding ocean is deeply connected to the territory's culture, food security and traditional way of life.Seumalu Elora Raymond of Fa'asao Amerika Samoa accused the federal government of "ignoring the voices of the very people whose waters, traditions and livelihoods are on the line."The territorial government has banned deep-sea mining within its own waters, although the proposed BOEM lease blocks are located in federally managed waters farther offshore.Earthjustice attorney J.V. Langkilde described the industry as largely untested and warned that American Samoa could become an early proving ground for commercial deep-sea mining.The governor of American Samoa has 60 days after publication of the proposed leasing notice to submit comments.If BOEM proceeds, it must publish a final leasing notice at least 30 days before the auction, outlining the final lease boundaries, bidding process and conditions.The agency has also considered dividing the proposed area into five leases of nearly 7 million acres each, though the final configuration has yet to be determined.While commercial mining is not imminent, the proposal marks one of the most significant advances in U.S. efforts to develop deep-sea mineral resources. The outcome could shape future policy on seabed mining at a time when more than 43 countries have called for a moratorium, precautionary pause or outright ban on commercial deep-sea mining until stronger international rules are in place.
Article Summary: US plans to auction up to 33 million acres of deep ocean around American Samoa for mineral exploration despite major environmental data gaps. The proposal marks a significant milestone in the country's efforts to secure critical mineral supplies for clean energy, electronics and national security. If approved, the lease sale is scheduled for November 19, 2026.

Article Title: Russia's overnight ballistic missile and drone attack on Ukraine capital Kyiv kills 9
Article Text:
Fire breaks out at Moscow's St Basil's Cathedral

At least nine people were killed and twenty-eight others were injured after Russia launched a barrage of ballistic missiles and drones targeting Ukraine's capital Kyiv overnight into Saturday. The attack damaged residential buildings, sparked multiple fires across the city and left people trapped under debris, officials said.Kyiv mayor Vitalii Klitschko had earlier said a five-storey residential building in the Solomianskyi district was struck by falling debris, causing severe damage and trapping residents inside."The first and second floors of the damaged residential building had partially collapsed," Klitschko said in a post on Telegram, adding that a fire had also broken out in the courtyard.Klitschko had said at least three people had been killed in the Russian missile attack and confirmed that several people remained trapped in the partially collapsed building. He added that five people had been hospitalised following the strikes.People were also believed to be trapped in another residential building in the Shevchenkivskyi district after the first and second floors partially collapsed, Klitschko said.Additionally, seven people were killed and 14 others injured in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district after the attack sparked fires and damaged homes, vehicles, an administrative building and other non-residential structures, emergency services told news agency AP.According to Reuters witnesses, more than a dozen explosions reverberated across the Ukrainian capital during the attack. This comes as Russia stepped up strikes on Kyiv in recent months, while Ukraine continues to face a shortage of air defence systems capable of intercepting ballistic missiles, which travel several times faster than the speed of sound.The latest bombardment came just two days after another large-scale Russian ballistic missile and drone attack across Ukraine killed 10 civilians and wounded more than 50 others. During that attack, a Russian missile also briefly entered Polish airspace.As Russian aerial attacks intensified, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy reiterated Kyiv's demand for additional Patriot air defence systems from the United States and its Western allies."The Russian air strikes on our country continue and air defense, specifically interceptors for Patriot systems against ballistic missiles, remains a top priority," Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram on Friday.The Ukrainian president also said he had spoken with US vice president JD Vance after his meeting earlier this week in Washington with president Donald Trump.The renewed appeal comes amid uncertainty over future US military support. At the Nato summit in Ankara in July, president Trump said the United States would grant Ukraine a licence to manufacture Patriot systems. However, during a Cabinet meeting at the presidential retreat at Camp David on Friday, Trump indicated that no final decision had yet been taken on the proposal.Meanwhile, a fire broke out at St Basil's Cathedral on Moscow's Red Square early Saturday before being brought under control, according to Russia's state-run TASS news agency.TASS, citing operational services, said the blaze started in the director's office on the first floor."On the first floor, in the director's office, personal belongings and furniture caught fire. The area of the fire was around 10 sq. metres," a source told the agency, as reported by Kyiv Post.The cause of the fire was not immediately known. No injuries were reported. Around 10 fire engines were deployed to the site before operational services confirmed that the fire had been extinguished, TASS said.
Article Summary: Russia launches barrage of ballistic missiles and drones targeting Ukraine's capital Kyiv. Attack damages residential buildings, sparks multiple fires and leaves people trapped under debris. Ukrainian president reiterates demand for additional Patriot air defence systems from the United States. Fire breaks out at Moscow's St Basil's Cathedral.

Article Title: 'Double tap': How terrorists are trapping Pakistan's security personnel
Article Text:
The latest assault came on Sunday, when a suicide bomber struck outside a police station in Swat's Kabal town during an anti-terror rally

A 'double tap' strategy to maximise casualties

Recent attacks expose worsening security crisis

Poll Vote & Share your view What should be the top priority to tackle rising security threats? Stronger intelligence and prevention Better emergency response 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan's security forces are increasingly facing a deadly challenge as militant groups adopt a "double tap" strategy that turns rescue missions into ambushes. The tactic, analysed by Pakistani newspaper Dawn, involves an initial attack on a police or security installation, followed by a second strike targeting reinforcements rushing to the scene.The evolving strategy has coincided with a sharp rise in militant violence, particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where police and military personnel have repeatedly come under attack in recent months. The latest assault came on Sunday, when a suicide bomber struck outside a police station in Swat's Kabal town during an anti-terror rally, killing at least 14 people, including police personnel, and injuring 18 others.According to an analysis by Dawn, militants have refined their tactics by carrying out coordinated two-stage attacks aimed at inflicting the highest possible casualties on responding security forces.The first team attacks a police station, checkpost or security installation, drawing personnel into a firefight. Simultaneously, another militant group positions itself along likely reinforcement routes.As additional police or military teams rush to assist, they are targeted through improvised explosive devices (IEDs), roadside ambushes or quadcopters capable of dropping explosives.Dawn said predictable response patterns have repeatedly turned reinforcement teams into easy targets. Over the past three years, at least 16 police personnel, including three deputy superintendents of police (DSPs), have been killed while responding to attacks rather than during the initial assault.The newspaper pointed to the July 29 attack in Hangu district as the latest example. Terrorists first stormed a police checkpost before attacking the reinforcements sent to support officers already under fire. Nine police personnel, including DSP Diyar Khan, were killed and 28 others injured. According to Dawn, it was the third major incident in which the second phase of the attack caused the heaviest losses.The pattern dates back to January 2023, when DSP Sardar Hussain and two of his guards were killed in an IED blast while responding to an attack on the Sarband police station near Peshawar.The strategy has unfolded alongside a broader escalation in militant attacks across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.On July 24, at least 15 people, including 14 security personnel, were killed after Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) militants attacked a joint police checkpost in Tank district. According to Pakistan's military, the attackers first attempted to breach the facility but were repelled before ramming an explosives-laden vehicle into the perimeter wall, triggering a massive blast that destroyed much of the checkpost. Security forces said 15 militants were killed during the operation, while 12 soldiers, two policemen and a forest department official lost their lives.Sunday's suicide bombing in Swat further highlighted the deteriorating security environment. The attacker detonated explosives after police attempted to stop and search him outside the Kabal police station, according to Dawn. The blast occurred near a large public demonstration where residents had gathered to protest the resurgence of militancy and demand stronger state action.Speakers at the rally criticised authorities for failing to curb militant activity and urged the government to restore lasting peace in the valley, which was once cleared of insurgents after a major military operation but has seen renewed militant activity in recent months.Data cited by Dawn from the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies showed that Khyber Pakhtunkhwa recorded 154 terrorism-related deaths in July, more than double the 75 fatalities reported in June, underscoring the rapidly worsening security situation.
Article Summary: Pakistan's security forces are increasingly facing a deadly challenge. Militants adopt a 'double tap' strategy that turns rescue missions into ambushes. The tactic involves an initial attack on a police or security installation, followed by a second strike targeting reinforcements rushing to the scene.

Article Title: US, Israel weigh bombarding Iran's energy infrastructure through the weekend: Report
Article Text:
US, Israel eye weekend bombing campaign on Iran's energy sites

The United States and Israel are planning a potential bombing campaign targeting Iran's energy infrastructure, with strikes possibly taking place over the weekend, CBS News reported on Friday, citing sources.However, US president Donald Trump has not yet given final approval for the operation.According to multiple US sources, officials have discussed wrapping up the operation before financial markets open on Monday amid concerns over the potential impact of the strikes on the US and global economy.However, no firm timeline has been finalised.The sources added that Israeli officials have been informed of the plans and are coordinating closely with the United States.A joint operation would mark Israel's return to active military operations after it paused its campaign during the US-brokered truce.Iran, meanwhile, has not launched attacks against Israel since the memorandum of understanding collapsed and the United States resumed combat operations in early July."Israel is unaware of a decision to restart full military operations, nor has been requested of Israel to join any military actions against Iran," an Israeli official was quoted as saying by CBS News.The development comes as Trump warned on Friday that Iran could be hit "very hard.""We'll be hitting him very hard and, you know, at some point they're going to say, 'We just can't take it anymore'," the US president said.The Wall Street Journal also reported that Trump had ordered preparations for a fresh military offensive aimed at pressuring Tehran into surrender, with the operation potentially beginning as early as this weekend.More than five months after the conflict began on February 28, when the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran, the fighting shows no sign of easing, with both sides continuing to exchange attacks.Throughout the conflict, Trump has repeatedly threatened to target Iran's critical infrastructure. Last week, he warned that the United States would destroy a bridge or power plant each time commercial shipping in the strategically important Strait of Hormuz came under attack.The latest report also comes days after Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu met Trump and US defence secretary Pete Hegseth in Washington.
Article Summary: US, Israel eye weekend bombing campaign on Iran's energy sites, sources say. US president Donald Trump has not yet given final approval for the operation. Israeli officials have been informed of the plans and are coordinating closely with the United States. A joint operation would mark Israel's return to active military operations.

Article Title: Pakistan restricts digital news websites reporting on PoK protests, crackdowns: Report
Article Text:
Pakistan expands online curbs following coverage of PoK unrest

Pakistan has reportedly expanded digital censorship measures by restricting access to several news websites following extensive media coverage of the ongoing unrest in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK).Alongside the reported blocking of local and regional news websites, international broadcasters, have also become inaccessible to users in parts of Pakistan, according to media reports cited by ANI.The restrictions appear to target platforms covering the recent protests, alleged security crackdowns and growing public discontent in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK). Pakistani authorities have not officially confirmed the reported restrictions.The channels facing possible blocking include those linked to Pakistan's main opposition party, its leader and jailed former prime minister Imran Khan, as well as several journalists critical of the government, according to a court order dated June 24.Earlier in July, Al Jazeera reported that a judicial magistrate's court in Islamabad had ordered the blocking of several YouTube channels based on a June 2 report by Pakistan's National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA).The agency alleged that the channels had published content that was "intimidating", "provocative" and "derogatory" towards state institutions and public officials.Al Jazeera reported that digital rights groups have warned the proposed bans could further restrict freedom of expression in Pakistan. With television and print media facing significant curbs, social media remains one of the few platforms for public debate and dissent, the report said.The broadcaster also reported that YouTube had notified 27 content creators that their channels could be blocked if they failed to comply with the court's directives.The restrictions come amid heightened sensitivity over the flow of information related to the political situation and local protests in PoK.The second phase of elections in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK) was marred by widespread disruptions, logistical challenges and continuing protests, raising fresh concerns over the credibility of the electoral process.Polling was held across 21 constituencies, including nine in the Muzaffarabad Division of PoK and 12 refugee constituencies located in different parts of Pakistan.Voting was disrupted in several constituencies as road blockades and protests affected access to polling stations and delayed the electoral process.
Article Summary: Pakistani authorities have not officially confirmed the reported restrictions. The restrictions appear to target platforms covering the recent protests, alleged security crackdowns and growing public discontent in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK) Earlier in July, a judicial magistrate's court in Islamabad ordered the blocking of several YouTube channels.

Article Title: Prank or emergency? US screening of Spiderman forces hundreds to evacuate after fart attack - watch
Article Text:
The person responsible has not been identified. Reports suggested that the smell may have been caused by a stink bomb set off as a prank (Photo: X/ColombiaOscura)

Hundreds of film fans were reportedly evacuated midway through the screening of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” in the USA’s Colombia on Sunday amid a foul fart odour spreading in the multiplex.According to the New York Post, the screening was progressing normally until halfway through the film, when an audience member allegedly released an overpowering smell that quickly spread through the darkened auditorium.The foul odour reportedly became so unbearable that hundreds of viewers left their seats and were evacuated into the cinema corridor. Although the screening was not officially cancelled, many audience members reportedly chose to leave before the film ended because of the lingering odour.The person responsible has not been identified. Reports suggested that the smell may have been caused by a stink bomb set off as a prank, or by a filmgoer who was unable to reach the bathroom in time.Several viewers criticised the unidentified culprit on social media.“There’s no respect anymore, but I don’t think anyone is so rotten as to evacuate an entire auditorium”, one person reportedly said.“To ruin a whole cinema like that, only God knows what that person ate”, another wrote.Others jokingly described the anonymous offender as the film’s real “villain”.The film itself, however, appears to have received a far warmer response. “Spider-Man: Brand New Day”, which stars Tom Holland, was rated “Certified Fresh” by 90 per cent of critics and received a 98 per cent audience score on Rotten Tomatoes.Film critic Johnny Oleksinski compared the movie’s tone with the Tobey Maguire-led “Spider-Man” films of the 2000s, which he described as the gold standard not only for Spider-Man movies but also for Marvel films.
Article Summary: Hundreds of film fans were reportedly evacuated midway through the screening of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ in Colombia. Reports suggested that the smell may have been caused by a stink bomb set off as a prank, or by a filmgoer who was unable to reach the bathroom in time.

Article Title: Indian-origin man among 25 facing US citizenship revocation over alleged fraud
Article Text:
The DOJ has filed a civil complaint against 65-year-old Narinder Singh in the District of Delaware

An Indian-origin man is among 25 naturalised US citizens facing proceedings to revoke their American citizenship over allegations including identity fraud, attempted murder, child sexual abuse and other serious offences, the US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced.The DOJ has filed a civil complaint against 65-year-old Narinder Singh in the District of Delaware, alleging that he used a fraudulent identity to gain admission to the United States. According to the department, Singh used two different identities from 1996 onwards before becoming a naturalised US citizen on May 1, 2008.The complaint alleges seven counts against Singh, accusing him of making multiple misrepresentations and engaging in unlawful conduct that reflected adversely on his moral character, a key requirement for obtaining US citizenship.Among those facing denaturalisation proceedings are also two people of Pakistani origin, Zia Murad Bhatti and Mohd Wasif, who are accused of using false identities.Announcing the coordinated action on Monday, Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said US citizenship was "one of our nation's highest privileges" and must be obtained "lawfully and honestly".He said the complaints alleged that the individuals secured naturalisation through fraud, concealment or other unlawful conduct, including hiding violent crimes, sexual offences against children, fraudulent identities and other disqualifying information.The 25 cases, filed between July 20 and August 3, involve naturalised citizens originally from 17 countries, including India, Pakistan, Mexico, Colombia, Nigeria, Jamaica, Taiwan, Jordan, Cuba and Sweden.Blanche described the action as the largest coordinated denaturalisation effort in the department's history, adding that it was "only the beginning". Since January 20, 2025, the Justice Department has filed 123 denaturalisation cases as the Trump administration intensifies efforts to strip citizenship from individuals accused of obtaining it unlawfully.The complaints cover a broad range of alleged offences, including attempted murder, child sexual abuse, domestic violence, marriage fraud, passport fraud, financial fraud and practising medicine without a licence. Civil Division Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate called it the "largest denaturalisation surge in recorded history".
Article Summary: Narinder Singh is among 25 naturalised US citizens facing proceedings to revoke their American citizenship. The DOJ has filed a civil complaint against 65-year- old Singh in the District of Delaware, alleging that he used a fraudulent identity to gain admission to the United States.

Article Title: US outbreak turns deadly: First two deaths linked to 'explosive diarrhoea'
Article Text:
Food safety measures under scrutiny During US outbreak.

Why are the deaths considered unusual?

Why is Michigan at the epicentre?

Can washing produce prevent infection?

How is lettuce linked to the outbreak?

Michigan health officials have confirmed the first two deaths linked to the ongoing cyclospora outbreak, a parasitic infection spread through contaminated food or water that can cause severe diarrhoea.The two individuals had “significant underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration”, the BBC reported, citing state health authorities.The foodborne illness has spread to 45 states, with nearly 7,000 laboratory-confirmed cases reported nationwide, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). While the outbreak has infected thousands of people, deaths from cyclosporiasis are far from common. The CDC says the illness is “not usually life-threatening”.Michigan is at the epicentre of the current outbreak, with state records showing more than 11,000 cases and 193 hospitalisations, although many have not been confirmed through laboratory testing.The heat-loving parasite infects the intestines and is transmitted through faecal contamination. Past outbreaks have occurred after people consumed fruits or vegetables irrigated with water contaminated by faeces.The CDC recommends washing all produce under running water, including items labelled as pre-washed.Washing alone, however, might not be enough to remove the parasite. The agency recommends cooking produce to a temperature of at least 70°C, or 158°F, which can kill the parasite.Officials have linked this year’s widespread outbreak to lettuce imported from Taylor Farms in Mexico, a key supplier to many food establishments in the US. US fast-food chain Taco Bell said it has removed lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms from its menu. Taylor Farms announced a voluntary recall of lettuce sourced from central Mexico.UK health officials have also warned about the outbreak following recent cases contracted by returning travellers.
Article Summary: The foodborne illness has spread to 45 states, with nearly 7,000 laboratory- confirmed cases reported nationwide. Michigan is at the epicentre of the current outbreak, with state records showing more than 11,000 cases and 193 hospitalisations. UK health officials have also warned about the outbreak following recent cases contracted by returning travellers.

Article Title: 25 US states sue Trump over fresh tariffs on 60 trading partners
Article Text:
25 US states has sued the Donald Trump administration over its new tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners.

A coalition of 25 US states has sued the Donald Trump administration over its new tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners, including India, calling them illegal and an attempt to replace earlier import taxes struck down by the US Supreme Court in February, The Guardian reported.The lawsuit, filed in the US Court of International Trade, seeks to block the tariffs, have them declared unlawful and secure refunds for duties already collected.According to the states, the tariffs imposed last month on 59 countries and the European Union cover 99.4% of US imports. The Trump administration has argued that the affected countries have failed to do enough to stop imports made with forced labour."After losing at the Supreme Court, the administration is once again trying to illegally raise taxes on families and businesses with a new round of tariffs," New York attorney general Letitia James said in a statement."No matter how the administration tries to justify it, the law and our Constitution are clear that the president does not have the power to impose sweeping tariffs on whatever countries he wants," James added.The states joining the lawsuit include New York, California, Illinois, Massachusetts, Washington, Wisconsin and 18 others, along with the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania.The tariffs took effect in July under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 after the administration's earlier "Liberation Day" tariffs were ruled unconstitutional.The new duties affect major trading partners, including Canada, Japan, Norway, Taiwan and China.The lawsuit follows a separate legal challenge filed by the Liberty Justice Center on behalf of two small US businesses, which argues that Trump exceeded his executive authority.Responding to the lawsuit, White House spokesman Kush Desai defended the tariffs."The United States is using its lawful authority to obtain the elimination of unreasonable acts, policies, and practices that burden US commerce," Desai said. "A foreign country’s failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labour is unreasonable and burdens US commerce, including American workers, and must be addressed. Section 301 tariffs have proven to be a legally durable tool since the President’s first term, and they remain so now. "New York Governor Kathy Hochul said the administration was using "forced labour" as a pretext to continue imposing broad tariffs that raise costs for consumers."President Trump’s illegal tariffs are nothing more than a tax on hardworking families, driving up the cost of groceries, household essentials, building materials, and countless everyday goods that New Yorkers rely on," Hochul said. "The Supreme Court has made it clear that this administration cannot ignore the law to impose sweeping tariffs."
Article Summary: 25 US states have sued the Donald Trump administration over its new tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners, including India. The lawsuit, filed in the US Court of International Trade, seeks to block the tariffs, have them declared unlawful and secure refunds for duties already collected.

Article Title: 60 venomous snakes, cocaine, guns and 22,000 dollars in cash seized during New Mexico drug raid; inland taipan among reptiles found
Article Text:
60 venomous snakes, cocaine, guns and 22,000 dollars in cash seized during New Mexico drug raid; inland taipan among reptiles found

Officials warn of danger posed by venomous snakes

Expert says inland taipan was the biggest concern

Snakes moved to licensed facility

Federal agents investigating an alleged cocaine trafficking operation in New Mexico made a shocking discovery after uncovering 60 snakes, half a pound of cocaine, three firearms and 22,000 dollars in cash during a raid on a home in the South Valley area near Albuquerque.According to KOAT Action News 7, the search was part of an ongoing federal investigation into cocaine distribution. While executing the warrant, authorities reportedly found an extensive collection of reptiles, many of them highly venomous and considered among the most dangerous snakes in the world.The seizure inventory included cobras, mambas, pit vipers and pythons, along with an inland taipan, widely regarded as one of the world's most venomous snakes. Officials also noted that several of the reptiles had names, including pythons called "Sunset" and "William" and cobras nicknamed "Blizzard" and "Pablo Escobar."The New Mexico Department of Wildlife said most of the seized reptiles are venomous and that bites from many of the species would require immediate medical treatment.The discovery has alarmed residents living near the property, particularly because of the potential danger if any of the snakes had escaped."There are a lot of kids here. And one of those goes out, and they're gone. I just stay away from snakes. I'm really upset," one neighbour told KOAT Action News 7.Professional snake wrangler Connor Sharp described the inland taipan as the most remarkable and concerning reptile found during the raid."Somebody having drop for drop the most venomous snake on the planet in captivity just outside of Albuquerque was pretty surprising to me, honestly," Sharp told the outlet.He added that the danger extends beyond the snake's venom because hospitals in New Mexico are unlikely to stock the specialised antivenom needed to treat an inland taipan bite."Probably no medical facilities in the state of New Mexico are going to have anti-venom that would be used to treat a bite from an inland taipan," he said.Sharp also noted that snakes generally avoid humans and rarely attack unless they feel threatened, explaining that they typically try to move away rather than bite.According to officials, the snakes were examined by professionals and appear to be in good health. They have since been transferred to a licensed facility while authorities work to identify permanent homes capable of safely housing venomous reptiles.Because each species requires specialised care and handling, officials said the animals will only be relocated to facilities with trained staff and appropriate safety measures.No arrests have been announced in connection with the raid.
Article Summary: 60 snakes, cocaine, guns and 22,000 dollars in cash seized during New Mexico drug raid; inland taipan among reptiles found. Officials warn of danger posed by venomous snakes in New Mexico. Snakes moved to licensed facility while authorities work to identify permanent homes.

Article Title: Man reunited with lost wedding ring after 10 years as 9-year-old niece makes incredible discovery in Minnesota lake
Article Text:
Man reunited with lost wedding ring after 10 years as 9-year-old niece makes incredible discovery in Minnesota lake

Nine-year-old niece finds wedding ring by chance

Family left speechless after decade-long search

Discovery brings joy after difficult year

A Minnesota man has been reunited with his wedding ring nearly a decade after losing it at the bottom of a lake, thanks to an unexpected discovery by his 9-year-old niece during a family vacation.According to the Pioneer Press, Stephen Meyer lost his wedding ring in 2016 while swimming with his son in Lake Belle Taine, where his family owns a cabin. The ring slipped off his finger and disappeared beneath the water, prompting years of unsuccessful searches by Meyer and his relatives.Despite returning to the lake every summer, Meyer was never able to recover the ring. His family also spent years trying to locate it, using magnets and even dredging the sandy lakebed in hopes of finding the missing band."I looked a lot. I go swimming every night," Meyer's mother-in-law, Malana Johansen, told the Pioneer Press. "We've spent a lot of time looking for that ring. We were dredging the sand. My neighbor gave me a big magnet. We could not find it."The breakthrough came on July 20 when Meyer's 9-year-old niece, Harper, visited her grandmother's cabin for the first time since she was a toddler. Unaware that a wedding ring had been missing for years, Harper was standing near the shoreline when she noticed something sparkling in the shallow water."She just picked it up and said, 'There's a ring!'" Johansen recalled.She explained that lower water levels caused by drought had exposed part of the shoreline, making the ring easier to spot."The lake has gone down probably about 30 feet since last fall due to drought conditions. It was still in the water, but she didn't really have to go in the lake to reach it. It was just there," Johansen said.Johansen said the family was stunned that Harper had found what they had been searching for over the past 10 years.Even more surprising was the condition of the ring after spending nearly a decade underwater."It just needed a little cleaning, but it looks gorgeous," she said.After losing the original ring, Meyer had purchased a replacement. He is now wearing both wedding rings.Johansen said the discovery meant even more because Harper and her family had endured a difficult year. Their home in Sierra Madre, California, was destroyed during the wildfires in early 2025."She has gone through quite a lot in the last year. To have this exciting thing happen, I think it's just wonderful," Johansen said.She jokingly suggested Harper could make a career out of finding lost valuables during her summer breaks."She wants to be a teacher, and she is going to be a fabulous teacher. But I told her, 'Then in the summertime, you should just offer to find things for people,'" Johansen said.Reflecting on the remarkable discovery, she added, "This is going to be family lore from now on."
Article Summary: Stephen Meyer lost his wedding ring in 2016 while swimming with his son in Lake Belle Taine. The ring slipped off his finger and disappeared beneath the water, prompting years of unsuccessful searches by Meyer and his relatives. The breakthrough came on July 20 when Meyer's 9-year-old niece, Harper, visited her grandmother's cabin.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Marco Rubio: 'God has blessed me in many ways but none more important than my wife Jeanette'
Article Text:
​Quote of the day by Marco Rubio

First meeting in Miami

Reconnecting and early dating

A traditional Catholic wedding

Life, family, and navigating politics together

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio wears many hats. But before all comes his family man image, as he always speaks profusely about his wife Jeanette and his children. In a social media post on his wedding anniversary, Rubio wrote: "The most important moment of my life happened 27 years ago tonight. God has blessed me in many ways but none more important than my wife Jeanette."Like Rubio, Jeanette was also born to immigrant parents. Her parents came to the US from Colombia.The story of Marco Rubio and Jeanette Dousdebes begins in the vibrant, close-knit South Florida community where both grew up. Born to Colombian immigrant parents, Jeanette was raised in Miami. In the early 1990s, she was a 17-year-old student at South Miami High School, which Marco had attended just a couple of years prior. Marco, then 19, was transitioning from his early college football days toward completing his undergraduate degree.They first crossed paths at a neighborhood party thrown by mutual friends. Though they were only loosely acquainted at the time, Marco was immediately taken by Jeanette. However, as is common with young relationships, life pushed them in different directions initially, and their real romantic story would take a few more years to fully spark.After high school, Jeanette enrolled at Miami Dade College and began working as a bank teller. In 1997, her life took a glamorous turn when she auditioned for and made the Miami Dolphins Cheerleaders squad, joining alongside her sister, Adriana. Jeanette even earned a spot in the team’s very first swimsuit calendar.It was during this time that Marco and Jeanette reconnected. Marco was finishing his law degree at the University of Miami School of Law, while Jeanette was balancing college, banking, and cheering on the sidelines at Sun Life Stadium. Having both matured, their casual acquaintance blossomed into a serious dating relationship.However, their journey wasn't without bumps. Early on in their courtship around 1995, the couple went through a temporary breakup. During their time apart, Marco spent nights going out to South Beach clubs with friends, but he quickly found the party lifestyle hollow.In his 2012 memoir, An American Son, Marco famously recounted a surreal night at a local nightclub covered in foam that ended up ruining his shoes. Standing in the foam, he had a moment of clarity, realizing that the party scene offered no real substance and that he truly wanted to spend his life with Jeanette. That very night, he walked to a nearby payphone and called her. The call led to a reconciliation that permanently cemented their commitment to one another.By 1997, Marco was ready to ask Jeanette to marry him. Wanting the proposal to be unforgettable, he planned a romantic trip to New York City during Valentine's Day weekend.He took Jeanette to the observation deck of the Empire State Building at sunset. With the Manhattan skyline behind them, Marco dropped to one knee and proposed. Jeanette said yes, and the couple returned to Florida ready to plan their future together.On October 27, 1998, Marco and Jeanette were married in a formal Catholic ceremony at the Church of the Little Flower in Coral Gables, Florida, a historic church that would remain a central spiritual home for their family for decades.Their wedding was a celebration deeply rooted in their shared Hispanic heritage and strong family ties, attended by large extended families from both sides.Shortly after marrying, Jeanette briefly studied fashion design at the International Fine Arts College. However, as Marco’s political career began its rapid ascent, first with his election to the West Miami City Commission, then to the Florida House of Representatives, and eventually to the US Senate, they decided to shift their primary focus to family life.Together, they raised four children: Daniella, Amanda, Dominick, and Anthony. While Marco spent long stretches away from home serving in government, Jeanette grounded the family in West Miami. She stepped out of the political spotlight for the most part, focusing on raising their children, hosting home Bible study groups, and engaging in charitable work, most notably volunteering for Kristi House, a Miami nonprofit aiding victims of child abuse and human trafficking.
Article Summary: Marco Rubio and Jeanette Dousdebes were married on October 27, 1998. The couple met in the early 1990s when Jeanette was a 17-year-old student at South Miami High School. They married in a traditional Catholic ceremony at the Church of the Little Flower.

Article Title: Man rejects Rs 2 crore offer in India and chooses $160K in the US because...
Article Text:
Man rejects Rs 2 crore job in India and accepts lower salary in the US.

A LinkedIn post comparing the salaries between India and the US triggered much debate as a man rejected Rs 2 crore offer in India and chose $160K in the US. A Dubai-based AI leader, CJ Teja Sai, shared the story of the US-based friend who made this decision to choose the US offer despite the huge difference in the cost of living. But the friend said he weighed in on the situation and made a calculated decision to stay in the US despite the visa anxiety. "In the US, I log off at 5 PM. In India, I'd be expected to be available 24/7," the man said. "Interestingly, he said he was okay with the visa pressure and uncertainty. For him, having predictable personal time mattered more," the post added."Then he shared a story from his uncle. His uncle works in the US. One of his friends, who was an engineering manager in India working closely with US teams, suddenly put in his resignation. When my friend's uncle asked why he was leaving, the manager shared what finally pushed him over the edge. A US sync meeting was scheduled for 3 AM India time. It was introduced as a 15-minute call. It finally ended around 6 AM. That wasn't a one-off. It was the expectation of always being available that made him resign," Sai added."That conversation made me realize something. When we compare offers across countries, we usually compare salaries and taxes.Maybe we should also compare time, boundaries, and the ability to disconnect. Compensation isn't just what gets credited to your bank account. It's also the life you get to live outside of work," the post read.The post triggered a major debate with many claiming that work-life balance is a myth even in the US. And if the person works in an Indian company or under an Indian boss, he will soon realize this, many argued. Some supported his decision and said that though he would be making less money in the US, he would get better lifestyle and better career opportunities in the US."Many times I had to extend my day. So work-life balance in the USA is similar to India," one wrote. "All the time he saved with work life boundaries in US he spent cleaning his house, washing dishes, taking out trash, cooking and cleaning," another wrote pointing out to the conveniences found in India.
Article Summary: LinkedIn post compares salaries between India and US. Man rejects Rs 2 crore job in India and accepts lower salary in the US. The post triggered a major debate with many claiming that work-life balance is a myth even in the U.S. Some supported his decision and said that though he would be making less money, he would get better lifestyle and better career opportunities.

Article Title: Americans discard around 50,000 mattresses every day; one recycling programme has recovered 650 million pounds from 17 million beds
Article Text:
Only a few US states have built systems to collect and recycle mattresses. (Representational photo- Getty images)

Mattresses create problems in landfills
