Steel springs damage heavy machinery

Since 2015, MRC has recycled more than 17 million mattresses and recovered 650 million pounds of material.

Mattress recycling programmes

Mattress recycling process

Limited recycling facilities

A mattress recycling programme in United States has recovered about 650 million pounds of materials from more than 17 million discarded mattresses, according to Product Stewardship Institute (PSI).Around 50,000 mattresses are discarded every day in the US, adding up to nearly 18 million every year. Most end up in landfills, even though more than 80 per cent of the materials inside them can be recycled.A mattress is one of the largest items most households throw away. It contains steel, foam, wood, cotton and fibre, all of which have value if they are separated properly. However, because these materials are tightly packed together, recycling them requires specialised facilities that are not available in many places.As a result, most discarded mattresses are buried in landfills instead of being recycled. According to a report by Ecoportal, only a few US states have built systems to collect and recycle them on a large scale, while much of the country still depends on landfill disposal.Landfills rely on heavy machines that compress waste to save space. The more rubbish they can squeeze into a smaller area, the longer the landfill can continue operating.Mattresses do not compress well. Even after being crushed by landfill equipment, one mattress still takes up about 23 cubic feet of space, roughly the size of a small refrigerator. When this is multiplied by around 18 million discarded mattresses every year, it uses up a huge amount of landfill space.Unlike many other types of waste, landfill space cannot simply be created whenever it is needed. Once it fills up, authorities must find new locations or expand existing sites.Mattresses also create problems for waste management equipment. Traditional innerspring mattresses contain steel coils. Instead of flattening during compaction, these coils often twist and become tangled.Steel wires can wrap around the moving parts of landfill compactors, including shafts and drums. Workers have to stop the machines and manually cut away the tangled metal before operations can continue.The same coils can also damage equipment at waste-to-energy plants, where rubbish is burned to generate electricity.Another issue appears after the mattresses are buried. Because they do not compress evenly, they leave empty spaces underground. Over time, these voids can cause the land above them to settle unevenly.These are the main reasons some US states introduced specific rules for mattress disposal.While most discarded mattresses still end up in landfills, some US states have developed recycling systems. Massachusetts banned the disposal of mattresses in landfills from November 2022.Meanwhile, California created a recycling programme funded through a small fee added when a new mattress is purchased. The programme began in 2016.By the end of 2023, the programme had recycled more than 10 million mattresses and recovered over 380 million pounds of steel, foam, fibre and wood, according to the report.Connecticut, Rhode Island and Oregon also operate similar programmes. These states report recycling rates that are much higher than the national average, which stands at around 19 per cent.A mattress contains several different materials that can be recovered. At a recycling plant, workers first cut open the outer fabric covering.The steel springs are removed and sent to scrap metal recyclers, where they can be melted down and used again. The polyurethane foam is shredded before being processed into products such as carpet padding.Cotton and fibre materials can be reused in industrial filters or insulation products. The wooden frame is chipped and later used as mulch or fuel.There are only about 61 dedicated mattress recycling facilities across the United States and Canada. This means recycling services are available only in certain regions. In many places, residents have no option other than sending old mattresses to landfill.Where recycling programmes do exist, many retailers offer take-back services when delivering a new mattress. For a small fee, they collect the old mattress and send it for recycling.If such services are unavailable, local solid waste offices may provide information about drop-off centres or scheduled collection days.
Article Summary: Around 50,000 mattresses are discarded every day in the US, adding up to nearly 18 million every year. Most end up in landfills, even though more than 80 per cent of the materials inside them can be recycled. Only a few US states have built systems to collect and recycle them on a large scale.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Serena Williams: "I really think a champion is defined not by their wins, but by…" - a powerful lesson on resilience and rising after failure
Article Text:
Serena Williams (Image: Wikipedia)

Quote of the day by Serena Williams

"I really think a champion is defined not by their wins, but by how they can recover when they fall"

The powerful message behind Serena Williams’ quote

Where this quote actually comes from

Why setbacks are simply part of any real journey

Why resilience matters more than being perfect

Why failure can end up teaching more than success does

Why real confidence comes from getting through hard things

Why persistence produces success that actually lasts

Why this idea clearly reaches well beyond tennis

A note on Serena Williams' journey

Other famous quotes by Serena Williams

Why this quote by Serena Williams continues to matter

Victories are easy to celebrate. What usually gets forgotten is everything that had to be survived first to get there. Serena Williams put that gap into words directly. "I really think a champion is defined not by their wins, but by how they can recover when they fall," she said. Across a career filled with genuine triumphs, she also faced injuries, defeats, criticism and long absences from the sport, and returned from every single one of them, which is really what gives this particular line its actual weight rather than treating it as a nice thing to say after a big win.Serena is redefining what greatness actually looks like. Most people associate being a champion purely with winning. She is arguing that real character shows up specifically in the moments of defeat, not the moments of victory. Everyone runs into setbacks eventually. Plans collapse. Mistakes happen. What actually separates people, in her view, is simply how they respond once that happens.Serena said this in a press conference following her win over Victoria Azarenka in the 2013 US Open final, the first women's final at that tournament in seventeen years to be decided over three sets. She went further in that same interview, saying, "I have fallen several times.Each time I just get up and dust myself off and I pray, and I'm able to do better or I'm able to get back to the level that I want to be on." She then named her own real example of what she meant, pointing to Muhammad Ali specifically, someone who spent years in prison and still came back as a champion afterward. "That really defines a champion," she said.Failure tends to get treated as something to avoid entirely. In reality, it is an unavoidable part of actually growing at anything. Every athlete loses matches somewhere along the way. Every entrepreneur runs into a genuine setback eventually. Rather than marking the end of progress, these moments usually provide exactly the lessons that later success actually depends on.Nobody gets to control every outcome that happens to them. What people can control is how they respond once something goes wrong. Resilience is really the ability to recover after real disappointment without losing hope or determination along the way, which lets someone adapt, improve, and simply try again. Champions were never actually perfect. They were persistent.Success mostly just confirms that whatever you were already doing worked. Failure forces real reflection instead, revealing weaknesses, pointing at real opportunities for improvement, and building a genuine humility that easy wins rarely produce. Plenty of life's most valuable lessons come specifically from the moments that felt disappointing at the time.Confidence does not only build through winning. It also grows through simply surviving something genuinely difficult. Every obstacle actually overcome becomes real proof that the next one is survivable too, which produces a kind of confidence considerably steadier than anything built purely on temporary success.Plenty of people stop after their very first serious setback. People who keep going despite real disappointment often end up achieving considerably more than they originally imagined possible. Serena demonstrated exactly this pattern repeatedly, returning from injuries, personal hardship and outright defeats to compete at the very top of the sport again and again.Although Serena is speaking from her own experience in sport, the same lesson applies everywhere. A student recovering from a genuinely disappointing exam result. An entrepreneur rebuilding after a real business setback. A family working through hardship together. Every meaningful goal eventually reaches a point where resilience matters more than raw talent ever could.Serena Williams is widely regarded as one of the greatest tennis players of all time. Across a career spanning more than two decades, she won 23 Grand Slam singles titles in the Open Era, while overcoming injuries, serious health complications and significant personal challenges along the way. Her repeated ability to return to elite competition after real setbacks has become one of the defining features of her entire legacy."The success of every woman should be the inspiration to another. We should raise each other up. Make sure you're very courageous: be strong, be extremely kind, and above all be humble.""Luck has nothing to do with it, because I have spent many, many hours, countless hours, on the court working for my one moment in time, not knowing when it would come.""You have to believe in yourself when no one else does.""I've grown most not from victories, but setbacks. If winning is God's reward, then losing is how he teaches us."In a culture that mostly celebrates only the wins, Serena's quote is a reminder that resilience genuinely deserves equal recognition alongside it. Winning matters. Recovering after losing tends to actually change someone. Real champions are not defined by a spotless record, but by their determination to get back up after every single fall. Ultimately, every setback carries the possibility of a stronger comeback for those willing to keep moving forward. Serena Williams' words remind us that resilience, not perfection, is the true measure of lasting success.
Article Summary: Serena Williams is widely regarded as one of the greatest tennis players of all time. Across a career spanning more than two decades, she won Grand Slam singles titles in the Open Era. She also faced injuries, defeats, criticism and long absences from the sport, and returned from every single one.

Article Title: Robbery attempt at Indian men waiting in parking lot after 11 pm, multi-city chase by police in Texas
Article Text:
A group of Indian people was waiting at the parking lot of a restaurant in the Colony when a black jeep came and the driver threatened them with a gun.

A multi-city chase took place in Texas after 34-year-old Ryan Edward Drouin, a known offender, threatened a group of men who were waiting at a parking lot of Sheesh Eatery & Lounge. According to reports based on surveillance footage of a restaurant, the incident took place on Juluy 29. These Indian men were waiting at the parking lot for their orders. The footage showed that a Jeep came towards them and they started running. Reports said the suspect lowered his window and displayed a firearm and demanded money from that group.The attempted robbery at the Colony, a city in Texas, was not successful but it was reported to the police and officers obtained the Jeep's license plate number from area surveillance footage and entered it into the Flock Safety License plate reader system. None of the Indian men were hurt.As the hunt for the gun-wielding culprit began, the cops found that the Jeep was heading towards Plano. Police tracked the vehicle to Drouin's father's home in Plano, from where Drouin again escaped and this started a vehicle chase.While the parking lot incident took place just after 11 pm at around 2.12 am, Plano police notified Richardson patrol units that they lost sight of the Jeep.Richardson officers tracked down the Jeep and attempted a traffic stop. But Drouin refused to pull over and then another chase started -- this time it went into Dallas.During the chase, Drouin fired at Richardson officers who returned fire. The pursuit ended near Alpha Road and Hughes Lane in Dallas after the Jeep became disabled. Officers took Drouin into custody at the scene, and Dallas Fire-Rescue personnel took him to a local hospital for treatment of a gunshot wound.Drouin has a lengthy criminal history with previous arrests including making a terroristic threat, burglary, and drug offenses. He's also been convicted of family violence assault in Collin County.The investigation involves all police departments as the Colony Police Department is probing the primary aggravated robbery investigation. The Dallas Police Department is leading the investigation into the officer-involved shooting because the gunfire exchange and arrest happened within Dallas city limits.
Article Summary: Ryan Edward Drouin, a known offender, threatened a group of men who were waiting at a parking lot of Sheesh Eatery & Lounge in Texas. The attempted robbery at the Colony, a city in Texas, was not successful but it was reported to the police.

Article Title: 44-year-old man climbs Brooklyn Bridge, strips naked, plants flags and jumps into East River; survives, identified and charged by NYPD
Article Text:
44-year-old man climbs Brooklyn Bridge, strips naked, plants flags and jumps into East River; survives, identified and charged by NYPD

Dramatic rescue after Brooklyn Bridge jump

Kazakhstan flag among those placed on the bridge

Multiple charges filed

A 44-year-old man miraculously survived after jumping from the top of New York City's Brooklyn Bridge on Sunday, authorities said. According to the latest update, the man has been identified as Galymzhan Abaildayev, a Brooklyn resident, who now faces multiple charges following the dramatic incident.As reported by the New York Post, the incident took place around 2.30 pm on Sunday when Abaildayev climbed the north tower of the Brooklyn Bridge on the Manhattan side, removed his clothes and erected several flags before leaping into the East River.Police said officers from the NYPD Emergency Services Unit attempted to persuade him to come down safely, but he jumped instead.Videos of the incident show shocked onlookers screaming as the man jumped from the bridge. He appeared to hold a piece of clothing or a bag above his head during the fall, seemingly using it as a makeshift parachute.Despite falling from one of the bridge's suspension towers, which stands about 278 feet tall, Abaildayev survived the impact.Harbor Unit officers quickly rescued him from the East River before he was taken to Bellevue Hospital, where he was reported to be in stable condition.According to the publication, Abaildayev allegedly placed several flags atop the bridge before jumping.Sources told the publication that one of the flags was the national flag of Kazakhstan, while another appeared to be a blanket with handwritten messages. Authorities have not disclosed what was written on it or the motive behind the act.The publication reported that police have charged Abaildayev with reckless endangerment, making graffiti, public lewdness, criminal trespass and disorderly conduct.The motive behind the incident remains under investigation.The incident comes less than a month after NYPD officers rescued a distressed woman who had climbed onto the steel cables of the Brooklyn Bridge and spent more than an hour trying to convince her to come down safely.
Article Summary: Galymzhan Abaildayev, 44, has been charged with reckless endangerment, making graffiti, public lewdness, criminal trespass and disorderly conduct. Police said officers from the NYPD Emergency Services Unit attempted to persuade him to come down safely, but he jumped instead.

Article Title: Chennai entrepreneur shares how he started business with ₹90,000 after quitting ₹1 crore US job
Article Text:
Vivek Thiruvengadam, the founder of Qubit Fitness.

Early challenges and gradual growth





Internet reacts





A Chennai-based entrepreneur has shared how he left a high-paying job in the United States, returned to India with his family, and started a business with savings of just ₹90,000.Vivek Thiruvengadam, founder and CEO of Qubit Fitness, shared the milestone in an Instagram post marking six years since he decided to leave the US after spending 14 years there."6 years ago, I took a leap that made no sense on paper, but made perfect sense in my heart. Sometimes, belief is your only business plan," he wrote.According to Thiruvengadam, the move was never about chasing a bigger income. He said he wanted to return to Chennai to be closer to family and create something meaningful. At the time, he and his wife relocated with their 11-month-old daughter.He said he launched Qubit Fitness in January 2021 without investors, employees or even an office."When I started Qubit in Jan 2021, I had no office. No investors. No team. Just my laptop, my time, and ₹90,000 in savings.".Before starting the business, Thiruvengadam had written down a personal goal of one day matching the income he earned in the US, but as an entrepreneur rather than an employee.The entrepreneur admitted the early months were financially challenging. He said his company generated ₹20 lakh in revenue by the end of 2021, which was only a fraction of his previous annual salary in the US."It was humbling, but it gave me belief," he noted.He said the business expanded steadily over the following years by adding more clients, improving systems and increasing its impact.Six years after returning to India, Thiruvengadam said he has finally achieved the financial target he had set for himself."Now, in my sixth year, I'm happy to share that I've reached that goal. Not as an employee... but as a business owner," he wrote.Reflecting on the journey, he said consistency and patience proved more valuable than talent alone."What I learned? Consistency beats talent. Patience compounds faster than effort. Money feels different when it's built from purpose," he added, while thanking his family, clients and early supporters for believing in him.The post drew congratulatory messages from users, with many praising Thiruvengadam's decision to return to India and start his own venture.One user commented, "Congratulations! Beautiful family. Wishing you much success."Another wrote, "Awesome journey man. Congrats on all your success, and best wishes going forward."A third user said, "Add to it anti immigration policies in US, the difficult lifestyle in US, sky rocketing healthcare, safety issues in US....my humble request is to encourage yourself and your kids to stay and serve Bharat and not migrate !"
Article Summary: Vivek Thiruvengadam, founder and CEO of Qubit Fitness, shared the milestone in an Instagram post marking six years since he decided to leave the US. He said he wanted to return to Chennai to be closer to family and create something meaningful. The entrepreneur said his company generated ₹20 lakh in revenue by the end of 2021.

Article Title: 'Long history of unlawful violence': Global watchdogs condemn Pakistan's crackdown in PoK
Article Text:
PoK (File photo)

As Pakistan-occupied Kashmir goes through its so-called assembly polls, reports of brutality, violence and unrest continue to surface, with global human rights and press freedom watchdogs raising alarm over an escalating crackdown on protesters and the media.International organisations, including Amnesty International and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), have flagged allegations of state-backed violence, restrictions on independent reporting, enforced disappearances of journalists and prolonged internet shutdowns. They have urged Pakistani authorities to end the crackdown, restore communication services and ensure transparent investigations into alleged human rights violations.Highlighting reports of excessive force used against demonstrators in Rawalakot, Amnesty International said the incidents reflected Pakistan's long record of using unlawful violence against protesters."The disturbing reports emerging from Rawalakot are consistent with the Pakistani authorities' long history of unlawful violence against protesters. A prompt, independent, and transparent investigation must be ordered into the security forces' use of force against protesters.So long as an internet and mobile services blackout remains in place, it will severely impede the independent verification of the full extent of the situation on the ground. We urge the Pakistani authorities to restore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area," Amnesty said in a post on X.Echoing similar concerns, CPJ said it was monitoring the deteriorating press freedom situation in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, citing internet blackouts, telecommunications shutdowns, reporting restrictions and the detention and disappearance of journalists.The press freedom watchdog also expressed concern over the reported disappearance of independent journalist Razi Tahir and his colleague Muhammad Saif, who were allegedly taken by men in police uniforms from their office in Islamabad on August 1."CPJ is deeply concerned by reports that independent journalist Razi Tahir and his colleague Muhammad Saif have been missing since August 1. They were reportedly taken by men in police uniforms from their office in Islamabad, and their whereabouts remain unknown. Pakistani authorities must acknowledge whether they are in state custody, ensure due process, and immediately release them if they are being arbitrarily detained," it wrote.In a subsequent update, CPJ said the two journalists remain missing while Kashmiri journalist Raja Ikram, who was reportedly detained in Islamabad on August 1, has since been released."Journalists Razi Tahir and Muhmmad Saif remain missing after reportedly being taken by men in police uniform on August 1. Pakistani authorities must acknowledge their detention if they are in state custody, ensure due process, and immediately release them. Kashmiri journalist Raja Ikram, who was reportedly detained in Islamabad on August 1, was later released," it added.CPJ also said the media crackdown appears to be extending beyond the region, pointing to reported action against major news outlets alongside continuing telecommunications disruptions.The criticism comes as casualties continue to mount during the ongoing protest movement. According to figures released by the Human Rights Council of Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir (HRC-PoJK) as of Sunday, at least 80 people have died, including 33 civilians before July 27, 43 people killed since July 27 across Rawalakot, Mirpur and Muzaffarabad, and four Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir police personnel.
Article Summary: Watchdogs raise alarm over escalating crackdown on protesters and the media. Amnesty International, Committee to Protect Journalists have flagged allegations of state-backed violence, restrictions on independent reporting and enforced disappearances of journalists. They have urged Pakistani authorities to end the crackdown, restore communication services and ensure transparent investigations.

Article Title: Indian agents killed over 30 LeT operatives in Pakistan since 2020, claims Lashkar leader
Article Text:
Picture from X

NEW DELHI: In what is being seen as a major public confession from within the ranks of Lashkar-e-Taiba , senior operative Rizwan Hanif has confirmed that more than three dozen terrorists linked to the outfit have been targeted and killed across several major Pakistani cities since 2020.Delivering a fiery, hate-filled address to a Pakistani audience, Hanif openly conceded that the terror group has suffered the loss of more than 30 operatives in recent years, using the platform to launch a sharp sectarian attack against other faiths while blaming foreign agents for the killings.Hanif claimed that Indian intelligence agents were responsible for the targeted killings across multiple Pakistani cities and region, including Peshawar, Karachi, Rawalpindi, Muzaffarabad, and Rawalakot.Addressing the crowd, he stated, "In the last four years, 30 of our people were killed by Indian intelligence agents—someone in Peshawar, someone in Karachi, someone in Rawalpindi, someone in Muzaffarabad, someone in Rawalakot.""Our only crime is that we believe in La ilaha illallah. We are not people who worship Hanuman, Ghanshyam, or Hariram. This Hindu wants the cow to be worshipped, the Jew wants the calf to be worshipped, and as long as a servant of Allah—the last Muslim—is alive, he will never allow the cow and the calf to be worshipped."The hate-filled address, marked by deeply offensive and provocative remarks against other religions, once again underscores how terrorist organizations manipulate religious sentiment to incite hatred and radicalize the public.
Article Summary: Senior operative Rizwan Hanif has confirmed that more than three dozen terrorists linked to Lashkar-e-Taiba have been targeted and killed across several major Pakistani cities since 2020. Hanif openly conceded that the terror group has suffered the loss of more than 30 operatives in recent years.

Article Title: 'They'll arrest us at hospitals': PoK protesters risk death over electricity, flour demands
Article Text:
Dozens killed in PoK as protesters treating gunshot wounds in makeshift clinics avoid hospitals for fear of arrest

Makeshift clinic treats dozens of critically injured

JAAC and authorities trade accusations

Food shortages, roadblocks add to tensions

A protest movement in PoK has escalated into deadly clashes between security forces and demonstrators, with dozens of people reportedly killed across the region in recent weeks, the BBC reported.The protests have been led by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), which has been demanding cheaper electricity and flour as well as better access to education, healthcare and other basic services. The movement says an agreement reached with the governments of Pakistan and PoK in October to address some of its demands has not been implemented.The BBC reported that Rawalakot, one of the main centres of the protests, was experiencing severe disruption, with roads blocked, shops shut and internet access cut off.The BBC visited a makeshift clinic near the main protest site, where a spare bedroom had been converted into a medical supply area and a bed placed outside beneath a tarpaulin was being used to treat injured protesters.A doctor identified by the BBC as Dr Anwar said the clinic had treated around 50 to 60 critically injured people since July 27, including an estimated 15 to 20 people with gunshot wounds.The doctor said the facility could provide basic emergency treatment, including stopping bleeding, dressing wounds and removing superficial bullets, but lacked the equipment required for serious injuries involving the chest, abdomen, head or other vital organs.He also said protesters were reluctant to seek treatment at the main hospital because of fears they could be arrested or shot there. Authorities have rejected that claim.The BBC spoke to families who said relatives had been shot during the protests. One woman, identified as Asma, said she was at a demonstration when she learned that her only son had been shot. Another man, Salman, told the BBC that his younger brother had died.The JAAC says its demonstrations are peaceful and focused on economic and basic-rights demands. The group has rejected allegations that it is responsible for violence, while authorities have accused it of being armed and attempting to disrupt ongoing elections in the region.The JAAC was banned in June and labelled foreign-funded terrorists by the authorities, according to the BBC. The group rejected the characterisation and said its financial support was from the PoK diaspora and not India, an accusation that Pakistan has tried to make on multiple occasions.Authorities have also accused the group of attacking law-enforcement personnel and obstructing public order. Officials have released drone footage that they said showed JAAC members carrying guns on rooftops and displayed weapons they said had been recovered from the group.The government has rejected allegations that security forces fired indiscriminately at peaceful protesters, saying law-enforcement personnel acted against people involved in attacks on security forces, threats to public safety or obstruction of lawful authority.The JAAC, meanwhile, has alleged that security forces were responsible for firing on protesters. Umar Nazir, a member of the group's core committee, also alleged that people had infiltrated the movement and may have carried out violence to support the authorities' narrative, though he provided no evidence for the claim.The BBC said that during protests it attended, its journalists saw no weapons or shooting among demonstrators, although gunshots were heard overnight and it could not establish who was firing or at what.The unrest has also disrupted supplies in Rawalakot. The BBC reported seeing food shortages, with most shops closed and protesters sharing available food. Some residents described attempts to smuggle rice into the city.Several roads have been blocked by fallen trees and other debris. Authorities have blamed the JAAC for the blockades, while also denying that they were preventing food or medical supplies from reaching Rawalakot.The protests come as local elections are taking place in PoK, adding another layer of tension to the confrontation.
Article Summary: Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) has been demanding cheaper electricity and flour as well as better access to education, healthcare and other basic services. The BBC visited a makeshift clinic near the main protest site, where a spare bedroom had been converted into a medical supply area. A doctor said the clinic had treated around 50 to 60 critically injured people since July 27.

Article Title: '15-year-olds shot, only asked for basic rights': Inside the deadly PoK crackdown
Article Text:
Deadly clashes continue during protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir

'Most victims were 15 to 35'

'We are not terrorists'

Teenagers as young as 15 have been among those killed or seriously injured in a sweeping crackdown on protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), according to a report by the BBC based on the accounts of residents, doctors and families from the protest hub of Rawalakot. The demonstrations in Rawalakot by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) have turned deadly amid an ongoing security operation.The report said that dozens of people have been killed across the region over the past two months in clashes between security forces and protesters. The demonstrations comes as local elections are underway in the region.A doctor identified as Dr Anwar said that he had treated 50 to 60 critically injured patients since July 27, including 15 to 20 people with gunshot wounds."Most of those who have been killed or seriously injured are young people between about 15-16 years old and 32-35 years old. I have seen very few patients over the age of 40," BBC quoted the doctor saying.According to the report, many injured protesters have avoided government hospitals fearing arrest or being shot, a claim denied by the authorities.Families of those killed described the protests as a movement for basic rights, including affordable electricity, flour, education and healthcare."We only asked for affordable flour, electricity and our basic rights," Ali, whose friend Shafqat Hussain was fatally shot, told the BBC. "Instead, our brothers are being killed. What was our crime? Why are live bullets being fired at us?"Asma, whose only son was killed, said: "We were only asking for our rights. We are not terrorists." She added, "He knew there were risks, but he believed standing up for justice was important. He used to say that dying for a just cause was an honour."Another resident, Salman, whose younger brother died during the protests, told the BBC: "He was the youngest in the family and was loved by everyone... I feel proud that he gave his life while standing up for the rights of the people. He was not fighting or attacking anyone."The JAAC says the protests stem from the government's failure to implement an agreement signed in October that promised relief on electricity prices and other public welfare issues.The group, which was banned in June and designated by authorities as a foreign-funded terrorist organisation, denies the allegation, insisting it is a peaceful movement funded by the PoK diaspora.The Pakistan-occupied Kashmir government has rejected allegations that security forces fired indiscriminately at peaceful protesters. It said law enforcement acted only against individuals involved in attacks on security personnel, threats to public safety or obstruction of lawful authority.
Article Summary: Dozens of people have been killed across the region over the past two months in clashes between security forces and protesters. The demonstrations in Rawalakot by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) have turned deadly amid an ongoing security operation. The Pakistan-occupied Kashmir government has rejected allegations that security forces fired indiscriminately at peaceful protesters.

Article Title: 'Do not befriend Kaafirs': Pakistani general levels terror allegations against India
Article Text:
Pakistan's military spokesperson Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry

Pakistan's military spokesperson, Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, has sparked controversy after saying in a video that Muslims should not befriend "kaafirs" (non-believers), warning that those who do would no longer be considered among the faithful."Do not befriend kaafirs (non-believers) and leave the faithful. If you do that, there's a problem. Then you are not among the Muslims," Chaudhry said while addressing a press conference.“Now our population is 240-250 million people, and we still have four provinces. We have to see whether this is serving the purpose of good governance. That debate has to be sensibly held by politicians, by those in power, even those who have previously been in power, and those who are responsible to the people of Pakistan,” he added.The remarks were made during a wider media briefing that focused on Pakistan's counter-terrorism operations, the security situation in Balochistan, and the country's ties with Afghanistan.Taking a jibe at India-Afghanistan ties, Chaudhry claimed that the Afghan Taliban regime's "business" was terrorism, alleging that it used militancy to sustain its economy, state institutions and diplomacy.“Even their diplomacy is centred on terrorism. What is common between India and Afghanistan, except their DNA? The only thing common is terrorism,” Chaudhary said, as cited by Dawn.Chaudhry also claimed that around 300 Indian websites were being used to support terrorism-related activities in Balochistan, while more than 1,000 social media accounts and what he described as a "hostile diaspora" were involved in spreading propaganda linked to terrorism.“First, an event or incident is seeded, right or wrong, and then it is framed by initiators, who hand it over to amplifiers. Then mass amplification is done by mainstream Indian media, channels and their print media as well, from where it is picked up by international media, and then you take it and run it as facts," he said.The DG ISPR said the government was also working to strengthen the police force, including by deploying newly recruited assistant superintendents of police (ASPs) to Balochistan and providing bulletproof vehicles, among other measures.The remarks come amid a series of attacks on Pakistani security forces across Balochistan last month, with armed clashes also reported during military operations in the Mastung and Kech districts, according to The Balochistan Post (TBP).The insurgency in Balochistan has been led by several separatist groups, including the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), which has waged a long-running campaign against Pakistan's federal government. The group has frequently targeted security personnel and infrastructure in the province and has also carried out attacks in other parts of the country, including Karachi.According to Pakistan's 2023 census, Balochistan is home to around 15 million people and is rich in natural resources, including coal, gold, copper and natural gas. The BLA maintains that these resources should belong to the people of Balochistan and opposes the federal government's control over their extraction and the province's security.
Article Summary: Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said Muslims should not befriend "kaafirs" (non-believers) He warned that those who do would no longer be considered among the faithful. The remarks were made during a wider media briefing on Pakistan's counter-terrorism operations.

Article Title: Peace rally in Pakistan rocked by suicide blast; 14 killed, 20 injured
Article Text:
The blast occurred near Kabal Chowk, where residents had assembled for the 'Olasi Pasoon' peace gathering

PTM condemns attack on peace gathering

Death toll rises as investigation begins

At least 14 people were killed and 20 others injured on Sunday when a suicide bomber struck outside the Kabal Police Station in Pakistan’s Swat district during a large public rally against terrorism, police officials said. The attacker detonated explosives after officers attempted to stop and search him at the entrance of the police station, triggering panic among hundreds of demonstrators gathered nearby.The blast occurred near Kabal Chowk, where residents had assembled for the “Olasi Pasoon” peace gathering to demand an end to the recent resurgence of militant violence in the Swat Valley.Soon after the bombing, PTM Momand said its social media team was launching a campaign condemning the attack on what it described as a peaceful gathering.“PTM socialMediaTeam is launching a campaign to condemn the horrific bomb blast that targeted Apeaceful gathering of ‘Olasi Pasoon’ in Swat. People who assembled to demand peace wr met with violence instead. Initial reports indicate at least seven pple killed #StopStateTerrorismInSwat,” the group posted on X.Swat police spokesperson Nasir Iqbal Karimi confirmed that 14 people had died in the explosion. Earlier, Swat Deputy Inspector General of Police Fida Hussain said seven people, including four police officers, had been killed and 20 injured, but the death toll was later revised upward.According to Swat District Police Officer Umar Khan, the bomber blew himself up after police personnel tried to search him at the station gate. He said security forces had cordoned off the area and launched an investigation to gather further evidence.The attack took place as the final speaker was addressing the gathering, causing widespread panic among those attending the rally. Rescue teams, police and local authorities rushed to the scene, and the injured were taken to Saidu Sharif Teaching Hospital for treatment. No group had claimed responsibility for the bombing by Sunday evening.Before the explosion, speakers at the rally had condemned the rise in militant activity and demanded that the government ensure lasting peace in the region. They said their movement had a single agenda, the restoration of peace and the elimination of terrorism from Swat.The speakers argued that maintaining law and order and eradicating terrorism were the responsibility of the state, and warned that continued insecurity could fuel broader public unrest. They also criticised the authorities for allegedly taking action against peaceful citizens while militants continued to operate in the mountainous areas of Swat.“Our children deserve education, and our families deserve to live in peace,” one speaker told the crowd.“We have witnessed years of bloodshed. Our mothers, sisters, and daughters have suffered immensely, and we do not want another generation of widows and orphans.”The bombing came amid a sharp increase in militant violence across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. He directed the relevant authorities to provide the best medical facilities to those injured.“Terrorists will never succeed in their nefarious efforts to harm peace, national unity, and the writ of the state,” he said, adding that the sacrifices of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police were a “source of pride for the entire nation”.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa governor Faisal Karim Kundi also condemned the attack, saying, “Terrorists cannot demoralise the nation with cowardly attacks.”Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's chief minister Sohail Afridi sought a report from the provincial Inspector General of Police and offered condolences to the families of the victims. “The elements hostile to peace will never be allowed to succeed in their nefarious intentions,” he said.

Article Title: 'Double standards': Pakistan rejects UN report on civilian casualties in Afghanistan strikes
Article Text:
Pakistan denies UN report that documents civilian casualties in Afghanistan, calls it 'baseless'

What the UN documented

Pakistan disputes UN findings

Pakistan's wider counterterrorism campaign

Pakistan’s military has rejected a UN report documenting hundreds of civilian casualties from cross-border fighting with Afghanistan, saying its forces targeted only Pakistani Taliban hideouts and other militant infrastructure and carried out the strikes in self-defence.Pakistan’s military spokesman Lt Gen Ahmad Sharif Chaudhry on Friday dismissed the findings as “baseless” and said Pakistani forces had not deliberately targeted civilians during operations against the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which Islamabad accuses of carrying out attacks from bases in Afghanistan.Chaudhry said Pakistan’s military had targeted “hideouts and infrastructure” used by the TTP and that those killed in the strikes were militants. He said the operations were necessary to protect people in Pakistan from attacks originating across the border.The comments came after the UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) documented 499 civilians killed and 1,216 injured in cross-border armed violence between Afghanistan and Pakistan from October 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026.The UNAMA paper covering the latest quarter recorded 399 civilian casualties between April 1 and June 30 — 57 deaths and 342 injuries.Among them were 40 women and 112 children, including 26 children who were killed. UNAMA said the leading causes of civilian harm were airstrikes and ground engagements, and attributed all the cross-border civilian casualties it documented during the period to Pakistani security forces.The heaviest toll in the April-June period came from Pakistani airstrikes on June 28 in Paktya, Paktika and Kunar provinces, according to UNAMA. The strikes killed 28 civilians and injured 189 others, the report said.In one incident in Paktya's Chamkani district, UNAMA said a Pakistani airstrike hit a three-storey civilian residence. Residents gathered to rescue people trapped beneath the rubble, but a second airstrike struck the same location about 20 minutes later, while rescue efforts were under way.Chaudhry questioned the UN and Amnesty International reports, arguing that they relied heavily on accounts from Afghans despite what he described as restrictions on freedom of expression under Taliban rule.He also accused the Taliban government of allowing militant groups to operate from Afghan territory and said rights organisations had failed to adequately document attacks carried out against Pakistan.“These are double standards,” Chaudhry said, questioning how often rights groups had documented civilian casualties from US-led coalition airstrikes during the earlier war in Afghanistan.Chaudhry said Pakistan had recorded 3,145 terrorism incidents since January and that 2,084 militants had been killed, while 819 Pakistanis, including soldiers, police personnel and civilians, had died.He said Pakistani security forces had conducted 40,348 intelligence-based operations across the country during the same period.According to Chaudhry, Afghanistan-based militants had also carried out 28 suicide attacks in Pakistan since January. He alleged that many of those involved were Afghan nationals or people linked to Afghan security structures, and claimed some suicide bombers had been recruited from among drug users.Pakistan has vowed to continue its counterterrorism campaign, with Chaudhry saying the military would maintain operations against the TTP and affiliated groups.“We will continue these operations,” he said, adding that Pakistan was winning the fight against terrorism and would, “God willing”, win.
Article Summary: Pakistan’s military spokesman Lt Gen Ahmad Sharif Chaudhry dismissed the findings as ‘baseless’ He said Pakistani forces had not deliberately targeted civilians during operations against the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which Islamabad accuses of carrying out attacks from bases in Afghanistan.

Article Title: Rescuers find Nirmal Purja's body; all 10 climbers confirmed dead after avalanche on Broad Peak in PoK
Article Text:
Ten climbers, including Nirmal Purja, died in a Broad Peak avalanche. Search efforts continue for the remaining bodies after the incident.

Renowned British-Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja and nine other climbers swept away by an avalanche on PoK's Broad Peak have been confirmed dead, according to the Alpine Club of Pakistan and Purja's expedition company.Search and rescue teams are continuing efforts to recover the remaining bodies.The 10-member expedition was hit by an avalanche on Thursday while climbing Broad Peak in PoK's Gilgit-Baltistan region. Rescuers recovered three bodies on Friday after locating four, but harsh weather disrupted helicopter operations and delayed the search. Military-backed rescue teams resumed operations on Saturday."The world has lost one of mountaineering's greatest climbers," Purja's expedition company, Elite Exped, said in a statement. It added, "No words can ease the pain of this unimaginable loss."Confirming the tragedy, Alpine Club of Pakistan president Irfan Arshad Khan said, "The loss of these courageous climbers, who came from different nations united by their passion for the mountains, is an immeasurable loss to the global mountaineering fraternity."Paying tribute to rescuers, Khan said, "The mountains inspire us with their beauty, but they also remind us of the immense risks faced by those who venture into the high Himalaya and Karakoram."Earlier on Saturday, local police official Tahir Khan said the remains of Omani climber Nathira Ahmed were being flown to Islamabad, while the bodies of American climber Mallory Geis and Nepalese climber Bahadur Gurung remained at a hospital in Skardu.In a statement, Geis' family said, "Mallory was a bright light who was loved deeply by her family and friends. She will be profoundly missed."Purja, popularly known as Nims Dai, was a Nepal-born former British Army soldier who became one of the world's most celebrated mountaineers after scaling all 14 peaks above 8,000 metres in a record 189 days in 2019. The feat was documented in the Netflix film 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible. His record was surpassed in 2023.Describing Purja's legacy, Elite Exped said he was "a leader who inspired millions through his courage, humility and unwavering belief that human potential is far greater than we often imagine."The expedition marked Geis' first attempt at an 8,000-metre peak in PoK. It was also expected to be the final expedition for climber and guide Sakhi, who was also a geographer and high-altitude photographer, according to the Moving Mountains website.PoK's northern mountain ranges, including the Karakoram, are among the world's most challenging climbing destinations. Avalanches, falling ice and rocks, extreme altitude and rapidly changing weather frequently contribute to fatal accidents during expeditions.

Rescuers recovered three bodies on Friday after locating four, but harsh weather disrupted helicopter operations and delayed the search. Purja, popularly known as Nims Dai, was a Nepal-born former British Army soldier.

Article Title: Burnt-out vehicles, rock-strewn roads, heavy security: PoK votes in second phase amid unrest
Article Text:
The elections in Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir (PoK) have been overshadowed by violence, allegations of electoral rigging and reports of enforced disappearances

Heavy security, protests overshadow polling

India rejects PoK polls

Pakistan conducted the second phase of legislative assembly elections in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK) on Sunday amid fresh unrest, with residents reporting burnt vehicles, rock-strewn roads and heavy security across parts of Muzaffarabad following clashes between protesters and security forces.The voting is taking place in the second of three phases for the 45 directly elected seats of the 53-member assembly. However, the polls have been overshadowed by nearly two months of protests, allegations of election irregularities, political boycotts and a security crackdown.Residents of Muzaffarabad said fresh violence ahead of polling had raised concerns that the unrest would dominate the election process. Local reports described burnt-out vehicles, roads blocked with rocks and a strong presence of police, paramilitary personnel and army troops in several areas after clashes between demonstrators and security forces.Pakistan has deployed a three-tier security arrangement across PoK, with police, Pakistan Rangers, the Federal Constabulary and around 2,100 army personnel guarding polling stations.The elections come against the backdrop of sustained protests led by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), which has been demanding greater political freedoms, economic reforms and the abolition of 12 assembly seats reserved for Pakistan-based refugees.The group has also sought better healthcare, education, employment opportunities and reduced political privileges.JAAC has boycotted the elections, arguing that the reserved refugee seats allow Pakistan's mainstream political parties to influence government formation in the region.The protest movement has intensified in recent weeks after talks with the authorities collapsed, leading to large demonstrations, strikes and clashes. Polling in two constituencies was postponed because of the deteriorating security situation.Rights groups, including the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan, the United Nations and Amnesty International, have criticised the crackdown on protesters, internet restrictions and the ban imposed on JAAC under anti-terrorism laws.India has rejected the elections, describing them as a 'cosmetic' exercise aimed at legitimising Pakistan's 'illegal occupation' of the region.External affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the entire Union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, including areas under Pakistan's control are an integral part of India.He said the elections were an attempt by Pakistan to 'camouflage its illegal occupation' and conceal alleged human rights violations in the region."The current cosmetic electoral exercise is nothing but an attempt by Pakistan to camouflage its illegal occupation and hide its grave human rights violations in the region. The ongoing mass protest in the Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir is the direct consequence of its economic exploitation, its denial of fundamental rights to the people and its administrative oppression," Jaiswal had said earlier this week.

Residents reported burnt vehicles, rock-strewn roads and heavy security across parts of Muzaffarabad. The voting is taking place in the second of three phases for the 45 directly elected seats of the 53-member assembly. The polls have been overshadowed by nearly two months of protests, allegations of election irregularities, political boycotts and a security crackdown.

Article Title: ‘Cockroaches’ and crackdowns: Can Pakistan’s Gen Z storm the barricades?
Article Text:
Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and army chief Asim Munir

The warning from within

A year-wise snapshot of terror attacks in Pakistan, with 2025 recording the highest number in more than a decade.

The uniform behind the curtain

A country of fragmented rebellions

A terrorised society

The Global Terrorism Index 2026 ranks Pakistan as the country most affected by terrorism among 163 nations.

Where is Imran Khan now?

Beaten into submission

What’s next

Poll Vote & Share your view Would you support a unified movement from Gen Z in Pakistan? Absolutely Probably not 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Just look at what is happening in Pakistan -occupied Kashmir. People have taken to the streets over bread-and-butter issues and local election grievances. At least 40 protesters have died this week alone. To add insult to injury, Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif has described these protesters as “enemies” like India and ruled out dialogue with them."Its absolute disdain for the innocent people of PoK was laid bare when the defence minister branded the protesting civilians as enemies," external affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said. He said the “so-called” elections represented a “humiliating rejection” of the Pakistani establishment. "We urge that the international community should scrutinise Pakistan's actions and hold it accountable for its atrocities," Jaiswal added.And yet, the violence has barely registered internationally. Some foreign media outlets have offered customary coverage, often with the expected tilt, but it has largely been treated as business as usual in Pakistan. No professional outrage merchants or loud global campaigners have mounted a sustained protest against the conduct of the Pakistani army.Expectations from Pakistan are now so low that even the use of lethal force against its own people struggles to move the global news cycle.That silence says plenty about how the world views Pakistan. But the more interesting question is how Pakistanis see these protests themselves.Pakistan interior minister Mohsin Naqvi may have inadvertently supplied part of the answer.“Whether you agree or not, the system we have been living under has collapsed,” Naqvi said at event.But his most revealing remark came when he talked about Gen Z. “If these ‘Cockroaches’ get united, they can turn everything upside down,” Naqvi said.With around 60% of its population under 30 and an estimated 65-70 million people belonging to Gen Z, Pakistan appears, on paper, primed for a youth revolt. So why hasn’t Pakistan produced a nationwide Gen Z movement?Pakistan is a “hybrid regime”, as its own commentators describe it. Over the past two years, the army has moved beyond being informally supreme and begun formalising its dominance. A constitutional amendment created the post of chief of defence forces for the army chief, placing the navy and air force under him as well. His tenure was extended, and he was elevated to field marshal with what amounts to lifetime immunity from prosecution.None of this required a coup. It was delivered through a compliant civilian coalition of the PML-N and PPP that increasingly resembles the administrative wing of military rule rather than an elected government.The real genius of the military’s political arrangement has been its creation of an endless game of musical chairs. When one civilian face becomes unpopular, the establishment replaces it with another: the PPP, the Sharifs, Imran Khan , and then back again.This constant rotation serves a specific purpose. It prevents public anger from consolidating into a single grievance against the military establishment. Responsibility is repeatedly shifted to the civilian face of the day. When things go wrong, the answer offered is not structural change but another saviour, another party and another election promising to fix everything.For Gen Z, therefore, there is no clean and accessible target around which a national protest movement can form. A young Pakistani can be angry with a leader or political party. But the military, the country’s true centre of power, remains officially apolitical and practically beyond reach.Pakistan does not lack dissent. Its dissent is fragmented by geography, ideology and competing objectives.In Balochistan, the Baloch Liberation Army and its supporters are waging a separatist insurgency. The Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan is not fighting for democratic accountability; it seeks the imposition of Sharia law and the overthrow of the constitutional order. A Baloch nationalist, a TTP sympathiser and a university student in Lahore or Karachi protesting unemployment are unlikely to assemble beneath one banner or chant the same slogans.The state, therefore, does not need to defeat one unified movement. It only needs to prevent several incompatible movements from recognising that they are confronting the same power structure.That fragmentation also allows the establishment to treat every form of dissent differently: terrorism in one province, separatism in another, political disorder elsewhere and foreign conspiracy almost everywhere.Then there is the grim reality that Pakistan has become one of the world’s most terror-ravaged countries. The Global Terrorism Index 2026 ranked it as the country most affected by terrorism. Pakistan recorded over 1,000 terror-related deaths in 2025, its worst figures since 2013.This security crisis gives the army both political legitimacy and operational cover. Terrorism becomes the justification for an expanded military role, while dissent can be blurred with insurgency or branded “anti-state”. Extraordinary force is presented as an unavoidable response to extraordinary danger.The repression is often brutal but bureaucratically administered: Sedition cases, enforced disappearances, media blackouts, internet restrictions and the permanent threat of being labelled a traitor.Pakistan’s Gen Z has already seen what happens when a genuinely popular political leader crosses the establishment.For many young and urban Pakistanis, Imran Khan became a vehicle for expressing anger against a closed political system. His removal from power and the crackdown that followed offered a textbook lesson in the cost of direct confrontation.Look at where Khan is now. The hybrid regime is actively trying to neutralise the country’s most internationally recognisable political figure. If the establishment can do that to Imran Khan, what chance does an ordinary young Pakistani believe he has?If it comes to its survival, the regime would not mind killing even thousands.Reports of enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings of Baloch and Pashtun activists surface with alarming regularity. Students, political workers, journalists and human rights defenders are reported missing after alleged abductions. Some are later found dead, their bodies bearing signs of torture.Pakistan’s own commission of inquiry documented more than 10,000 cases of enforced disappearance between 2011 and early 2024.For young Baloch and Pashtuns, the message could hardly be clearer: Challenging the state may result not merely in arrest, but in disappearance.This explains why Pakistan may not witness a Gen Z uprising in the classic sense: Millions occupying the streets, facing down the state and forcing a negotiated reset.Naqvi is right about one thing: if Pakistan’s young people unite, they could turn the system upside down. That is precisely why the system has spent decades ensuring they remain divided, disillusioned and afraid.Elsewhere, Gen Z has taken to the streets to reclaim its future from misrule. In Pakistan, it is being taught that survival itself may be the most it can hope for.
Article Summary: Pakistan is a ‘hybrid regime’, as its own commentators describe it. With around 60% of its population under 30 and an estimated 65-70 million people belonging to Gen Z, Pakistan appears, on paper, primed for a youth revolt. So why hasn't Pakistan produced a nationwide Gen Z movement?

Article Title: ‘Dhurandhar’ gangster’s brother shot in Karachi
Article Text:
Personal enmity or gang war? Probe on into hit on Zubair Baloch

Zubair Baloch — the brother of jailed Pakistan gangster Uzair Baloch, whose ruthless ascent was dramatised in the movie ‘Dhurandhar’ — is learned to be critically wounded following a targeted drive-by shooting in Karachi’s Lyari neighbourhood on Thursday evening, reports .The 40-year-old was sitting outside his Singu Lane home when two masked assailants on a motorcycle opened fire, striking him in the chest and abdomen.Zubair was rushed to Civil Hospital Karachi for emergency surgery. Two bystanders were also injured in the crossfire, with one reported to be in serious condition.According to Pakistan police, the attackers fled after a nearby shopkeeper returned fire. CCTV footage from the spot, which surfaced on Telegram channels, showed chaos on the street as the gunmen escaped.Police told the local press they were probing angles of personal enmity and the potential resurgence of long-standing gang wars.Zubair, arrested in multiple criminal cases in 2012, was released from prison last year, while his brother Uzair remains in jail serving a 12-year sentence handed down by a military court.Uzair and several accomplices were indicted for a 2012 armed attack on law enforcement officers under Kalakot police station’s jurisdiction.In April 2020, Uzair Baloch received a 12-year prison sentence for espionage.For decades, the historic Karachi neighbourhood of Lyari served as the epicentre of a gang war and a hub of organised crime. The turmoil traces back to early turf battles over drug trade routes and extortion rackets, which eventually expanded into a high-stakes proxy war involving major political factions.Notorious figures such as Sardar Abdul Rehman Baloch aka Rehman Dakait and his fierce rival Arshad Pappu turned narrow alleyways into battlegrounds, leveraging strategic political patronage through outfits like Peoples’ Aman Committee to insulate their syndicates from police oversight. Following Rehman Dakait’s death in a 2009 police encounter, his cousin Uzair Baloch stepped in to control the dominant faction.
Article Summary: Zubair Baloch, 40, was shot in the chest and abdomen on Thursday evening. He was sitting outside his home when two masked assailants opened fire. Two bystanders were also injured in the crossfire, with one reported to be in serious condition. Police are probing angles of personal enmity and the potential resurgence of gang wars.

Article Title: Pakistan minister invokes 'cockroaches' analogy, says united Gen-Z can 'turn everything upside down'
Article Text:
Calls for new provinces and decentralisation

'Biggest supporter' of democracy

Youth want jobs, not handouts

'Cockroaches' remark

Business community urged to back reforms

Mounting debt concerns

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is more important for the youth? Merit-based jobs Welfare schemes Internships and training programs 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan interior minister Mohsin Naqvi on Thursday declared that the country's governance system had "collapsed", calling for the creation of new administrative units or provinces and urging political parties to reach a consensus on sweeping constitutional and governance reforms. He warned that without structural changes, Pakistan would remain trapped in recurring political and economic crises.Addressing the Pakistan Economic Summit 2026 in Islamabad, Naqvi said Pakistan's decades-old governance model had failed to deliver justice, economic opportunities or effective public services. He argued that decentralisation and the emergence of new leadership were essential to reform the country."Whether you agree or not, the system we have been living under has collapsed."Naqvi said repeated attempts to fix Pakistan's problems within the existing framework had failed, adding that the same debates would continue even a decade later unless the country's governance structure was fundamentally reformed."I believe the people responsible for bringing Pakistan to its current state are sitting in this hall," he said, adding that if a system had failed to function effectively for 70 to 80 years, there must be fundamental flaws in its design.The interior minister said the solution lay in decentralising governance through the creation of additional administrative units or provinces, arguing that local ownership would improve governance and allow new political leadership to emerge."The solution is only one.""You will have to take [the matter of] administrative units, provinces or whatever you may call it, to the public.""Unless units are made and they take ownership, and a new leadership comes, this will not happen."Naqvi urged all political parties to negotiate a comprehensive reform agenda instead of continuing with what he described as an outdated governance structure."All political parties should sit together in a single room, whether for a day, a month or a year. They will have to settle every issue of their country, including new units and provinces.""Unless they do so, unless they sit together and change this, this country will remain in the same condition, regardless of how many seminars and functions you hold."While describing himself as "the biggest supporter" of democracy, Naqvi argued that democratic governance could take different institutional forms and said Pakistan should not remain tied to a system that had consistently underperformed."We all want democracy. I am the biggest supporter of democracy and will remain so. But there are five or six systems within democracy. Yet we insist that no matter what happens, we must continue dragging along the same one."He also criticised policy failures, saying Pakistan continued to import agricultural commodities such as wheat despite being an agricultural country.Naqvi acknowledged the long working hours of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif but argued that the government remained focused on crisis management instead of long-term reforms."I have seen Shehbaz Sharif work 12 to 14 hours a day. He could even work 18 hours a day, but we are only firefighting.""Until you correct the basics of this country while adhering to the spirit of democracy, this will remain the same."Naqvi said Pakistan's young people were demanding merit-based employment, transparent recruitment and equal opportunities rather than welfare schemes or financial assistance."We think giving youngsters stipends of a few thousand rupees a month or tablets will make them happy, but ask them what they really want.""Their only demand is merit-based jobs and employment opportunities. They are not asking you for tablets or a few thousand rupees every month."According to the minister, Pakistani youth had the potential to earn between $2,000 and $4,000 per month if provided with the right opportunities.Referring to a term that has recently been used for Gen-Z in the wake of student protests in India, Naqvi warned that growing frustration among young people should not be ignored."If these 'Cockroaches' get united, they can turn everything upside down."He said the government should address the aspirations of young people before dissatisfaction intensified, arguing that their primary demands centred on merit-based jobs and equal opportunities.Naqvi also called on Pakistan's business community to play a more active role in reforming the country's political system, arguing that industrialists and traders had long been intertwined with politics."One gives funding of Rs500 million before elections, or the other gives Rs100 million or Rs50 million."He questioned why business leaders preferred financing political candidates instead of contesting elections themselves."Why don't businessmen enter politics? You are willing to fund politicians, but consider entering politics yourselves to be something shameful. You will have to stand up for yourselves."Highlighting Pakistan's fiscal challenges, Naqvi likened the federal government's finances to a household beginning every month already burdened with debt."The condition of this federal government is such that we make our budgets in the negative, and we discuss how much debt we have to incur this year.""[...] We will take more debts, but we will not correct things."He said leaders across the political spectrum understood the country's structural problems but had repeatedly failed to implement reforms, urging all stakeholders to build consensus on a long-term governance overhaul.
Article Summary: Mohsin Naqvi says Pakistan's governance system has "collapsed" Calls for creation of new administrative units or provinces. Urges political parties to reach consensus on constitutional and governance reforms. Calls on business community to play more active role in reforming the country.

Article Title: 34 killed as methane explosion tears through coal mine in Pakistan's Balochistan
Article Text:
Coal mine blast in Pakistan's Balochistan (AP photo)

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think the compensation offered to families of miners is sufficient? Yes, it's fair No, it’s inadequate 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

At least 34 miners in Pakistan were killed and 10 other remained trapped after a methane gas explosion ripped through a coal mine in Balochistan province on Thursday, as officials told news agency AP.While rescuers continued a race against time to reach those still underground.The explosion took place on the outskirts of Quetta, the provincial capital, and was apparently triggered by a buildup of methane gas, according to government mine inspector Ghani Baloch.Rescue teams initially recovered the bodies of seven miners before locating 25 more, provincial officials and the disaster management agency said in a statement. The search and rescue operation was continuing as teams worked to locate and recover the remaining trapped workers.Baloch said rescue efforts would continue until all those trapped were accounted for, but warned that the death toll was likely to rise.“The chances of finding anyone alive diminish after methane gas explosions because oxygen levels drop to zero, and rescuers are also proceeding cautiously inside the mine,” Baloch said.Authorities have begun handing over the recovered bodies to their families for burial, while relatives of the missing miners continued to wait anxiously for updates, Baloch added.Balochistan's minister for mines and minerals Shoaib Nosherwani said rescue personnel were operating under extremely challenging conditions.Nosherwani expressed condolences to the victims' families and announced that the provincial government would provide compensation of 500,000 Pakistani rupees (about $1,800) to the family of each miner killed in the blast.He said authorities would conduct a thorough investigation into the cause of the explosion and review mining safety measures to prevent similar incidents.Meanwhile, the Pakistan Central Mines Labour Federation alleged that negligence may have contributed to the disaster. In a statement, the union urged the government to strictly enforce mining safety regulations and take stringent action against companies that violate mine safety laws.Fatal accidents are frequent in Pakistan's coal mining industry, particularly in Balochistan, where many mines operate without adequate ventilation, gas monitoring systems or other essential safety measures.Labour groups and mine workers have repeatedly accused mine owners of ignoring safety standards and failing to provide proper protective equipment.Despite the hazardous working conditions and meagre wages, thousands of people continue to rely on coal mining for their livelihoods in Balochistan, Pakistan's largest yet least developed province, where poverty and unemployment remain widespread.
Article Summary: The explosion took place on the outskirts of Quetta, the provincial capital, and was apparently triggered by a buildup of methane gas. Rescue teams initially recovered the bodies of seven miners before locating 25 more. The search and rescue operation was continuing as teams worked to locate and recover the remaining trapped workers.

Article Title: 11 police personnel, 15 militants killed in overnight attack in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Article Text:
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (ANI file photo)

Pakistan suffered a major overnight militant attack on a police post in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, leaving 11 police personnel and 15 attackers dead by early Thursday.The attack targeted the Khazina police post in Hangu district, close to the Afghanistan border. Responding security forces fought back, killing 15 militants during the exchange of fire, police official Irfan Khan said.No group immediately claimed responsibility for the assault, though suspicion is expected to fall on the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has intensified attacks on Pakistani security forces in the border region in recent months.The dead included police officer Diyar Khan, who was leading a reinforcement team to the attacked outpost, according to a statement from the provincial police. More than two dozen police personnel were also injured in the fighting.Police said the militants used heavy weapons to storm the post. Reinforcements heading to the scene were ambushed on the way, with an armoured personnel carrier damaged before officers regrouped and engaged the attackers, eventually forcing them back.Pakistan has seen a steady rise in militant violence in recent years, with the TTP blamed for many of the attacks. Although the group is separate from Afghanistan's ruling Taliban. Since the Taliban returned to power in Kabul in 2021, Islamabad has repeatedly accused the Afghan government of sheltering TTP militants, a charge that Kabul has consistently denied.
Article Summary: Attack targeted Khazina police post in Hangu district, close to the Afghanistan border. Responding security forces fought back, killing 15 militants during the exchange of fire. No group immediately claimed responsibility for the assault, though suspicion is expected to fall on the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP)

Article Title: Bangladesh seeks India’s stand on Sheikh Hasina’s Aug 5 virtual address
Article Text:
Former Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina (AP image)

DHAKA: Ahead of former Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina ’s likely Aug 5 virtual address, state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam Monday asked India to clarify whether it supports the online meeting of the Awami League chief.The event at Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia in Delhi will be Hasina’s first public appearance, exactly two years after massive protests led to her govt’s ouster and she fled Bangladesh.“We are moving forward with India with a forward-looking approach. We don’t want it to be damaged, and I firmly believe that India doesn’t want it either. So, India has to clarify whether it is supporting it or not,” she said while addressing reporters at ministry of foreign affairs.Asked about Hasina and other Awami League members staying abroad, the minister stressed though Indian govt is not organising the programme, “India has to clarify because they are in India.”Meanwhile, PM Tarique Rahman’s foreign affairs adviser Humaiun Kobir, during a meeting with Indian high commissioner Dinesh Trivedi at Prime Minister’s Office Monday, said Dhaka expects New Delhi’s cooperation in ensuring that any person from the banned Awami League, including Hasina, does not use Indian territory to make political statements or conduct activities aimed at creating instability within Bangladesh.Shama Obaed said Bangladesh could “communicate” with India on the event if it considers it necessary. “Dhaka does not want the issue to undermine bilateral relations,” she said, claiming New Delhi had indicated it did not expect a fugitive accused to make political statements from Indian territory — Hasina has been sentenced to death.She said political activities by fugitives from India that seek to create instability in Bangladesh could negatively affect bilateral relations. Asked about the invitation to PM Tarique Rahman to attend Brics Summit in Sept in Delhi, she indicated no decision had been taken yet.
Article Summary: The event at Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia in Delhi will be Hasina’s first public appearance. It will be exactly two years after massive protests led to her govt's ouster and she fled Bangladesh. Bangladesh could “communicate” with India on the event if it considers it necessary.

Article Title: Watch: Broad Peak avalanche that killed record-breaking mountaineer Nirmal Purja and his crew
Article Text:
Footage captures the moment a catastrophic avalanche swept down Broad Peak on 30th July, resulting in 10 fatalities. (Source: @karakoramvision)

What happened on Broad Peak?

Who was Nirmal Purja ?

Pakistan-based tour operator Karakoram Vision said the visuals were captured from base camp on July 30 as the group climbed the mountain. It claimed an avalanche struck above the climbers and that no one was visible after the snow cleared. The visuals have not been independently authenticated.The avalanche at about 5,700 metres swept away the 10-member expedition on Thursday on Broad Peak, an 8,051-metre mountain in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir’s Gilgit-Baltistan region and the world’s 12th-highest peak.The group included climbers from Nepal, Pakistan, the US, Oman and China.Ground and military-backed rescue teams searched the mountain with helicopters and drones, but poor weather and hazardous terrain hampered operations. By Sunday, rescuers had located eight bodies, including Purja’s, while teams continued searching for the remaining two climbers and worked to bring the bodies down.Purja, 43, was a Nepal-born British mountaineer and former British Army soldier. He climbed the world’s 14 highest peaks in a record 189 days in 2019, an achievement featured in the Netflix documentary 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible. The record was broken in 2023.He was also part of the all-Nepali team that completed the first winter ascent of K2 in 2021.Prince William was among those who paid tribute, describing Purja as one of the world’s greatest mountaineers and offering condolences to the families of those killed.
Article Summary: Nirmal Purja, 43, was a Nepal-born British mountaineer and former British Army soldier. He climbed the world’s 14 highest peaks in a record 189 days in 2019, an achievement featured in the Netflix documentary 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible.
